articles.title: Lutnick under fire: How Trump’s commerce secretary cultivated Nvidia’s CEO while chip controls slipped
articles.summary: The first call, as Jensen Huang remembers it, came from Howard Lutnick.
articles.body: The first call, as Jensen Huang remembers it, came from Howard Lutnick. It was around the start of Donald Trump’s second term, and Lutnick was preparing to become his Commerce Secretary. His message to the head of Nvidia was simple: whenever you need the president, call us. Recounting the call on Joe Rogan’s podcast last December, Huang remembered fondly that Lutnick had called him and his company “a national treasure.” Two years later, Huang has resigned from Nvidia and Lutnick is under intense scrutiny for what some Trump advisers see as inaction in placing limits on US chip exports to China and his role in cultivating Huang as a top administration ally. Other administration officials have accused Lutnick of bucking internal consensus and Trump’s own directives in failing to blacklist an Nvidia customer suspected of funneling chips to China. Some of Trump’s advisers, reeling from the fallout of Huang’s resignation, have begun discussing whether Lutnick should be dismissed, according to people familiar with the conversations. This account is derived from more than a dozen sources, including officials inside the administration and the tech industry. They described a rapidly deepening relationship that came to influence nearly all areas of the White House’s stance toward some of the most powerful technology in the world. Questions surrounding the scandal — and the fresh push to limit sales of advanced chips to China — are likely to persist as Trump prepares to meet next week with Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Shenzhen, the hub of China’s tech industry. American officials said they didn’t expect Trump to raise the alleged spying with Xi, and said China wouldn’t have a say in whether Washington tightens restrictions on access to chips. ‘What the hell is Nvidia?’ Until shortly after Trump’s inauguration last year, Huang was nearly a stranger to Trump’s world. He would skip the swearing-in to spend Lunar New Year with employees in Asia, while his tech titan counterparts Mark Zuckerberg and Jeff Bezos had prime spots in the Capitol Rotunda. Trump, by his own account, had barely heard of Nvidia or its CEO: “What’s his name? What the hell is Nvidia?” he recalled wondering a few months later. “I’ve never heard of it before.” His ignorance wouldn’t last long. Eleven days after being sworn in for a second term, Trump met Huang at the White House. Huang also met that day with Lutnick, still awaiting confirmation as Commerce Secretary. As Trump signed executive orders in the Oval Office later that afternoon with the cameras rolling, he was full of praise for the man he’d only recently met. “He’s a great gentleman, and I hadn’t met him,” Trump said as he reflected on what he called a good meeting. “He’s the biggest in the world in terms of chips.” Over the next two years, the relationship would deepen over dinners, phone calls and many, many meetings. It was aided at every step by Lutnick, who helped elevate Huang’s profile and whose agency is responsible for keeping sensitive American technology away from adversaries. On Thursday, after Huang resigned from Nvidia following revelations he had extramarital affairs with two women, one of whom may be connected to China, Lutnick’s critics began circling. Administration officials who have long been concerned about Huang’s influence on Trump said privately that the Commerce Department failed to crack down on chip shipments to companies suspected of passing them on secretly to China. Speaking on CNBC Friday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said a wide swath of Trump’s administration — including the Treasury and State departments, the Pentagon and the US Trade Representative — favored placing the company at the center of the scandal, Megaspeed, on an export blacklist. He said it was the Commerce Department, led by Lutnick, that had failed to follow through. “Commerce…has the pen…and you will have to ask them about their internal process,” he said. Both Republicans and Democrats on Capitol Hill demanded Lutnick answer questions about what he knew, and when. House Foreign Affairs Committee Democrats wrote to Lutnick demanding to know what he and his export control chief, Jeffrey Kessler, knew about Megaspeed, and when. Senate Democrats directed Lutnick to preserve documents, communications and records related to Nvidia’s exports of advanced chips. And some Democrats went further in their criticism of Lutnick. “I think he should be fired,” Sen. Chris Van Hollen told ABC News in an interview that aired Sunday. Van Hollen, the top Democrat on the Senate subcommittee that oversees Commerce Department funding, is running to be Senate majority leader in the next Congress. “This news is as concerning as it gets,” Sen. Jim Banks, a Trump ally, said Thursday on Fox News. “When you’re in a war with another country, you don’t give them your best technologies. And that’s why lawmakers, for the last two years, have been pushing hard to stop our high-end computer chips from being exported to China.” The White House said Thursday Trump “maintains complete confidence in the secretary and his ability to carry out the position as the most transformative Commerce Secretary in modern history.” A deepening relationship A few months after Huang’s first Oval Office meeting, Lutnick played a role in facilitating Huang’s attendance at a $1-million-a-head MAGA Inc. dinner at Mar-a-Lago, according to two people familiar with the matter. The April dinner proved fateful. Huang used it to make a final appeal against planned restrictions on selling Nvidia’s H20 chip to Chinese customers. Trump, meanwhile, walked away impressed with his new, extraordinarily wealthy friend. Huang’s charm offensive at the Palm Beach dinner seemed to work, but only briefly. The White House moved to shelve the planned curbs. But as a trade war with China heated up, Nvidia later disclosed that the government had told it that H20 sales to China would require a license – and that the requirement would stay in place indefinitely. Huang kept working at it. At an Investing in America event at the end of April 2025, Lutnick and Huang were photographed together in the Cross Hall. Trump turned the moment into a show of affection. “I could have Jensen negotiating. He’d blow my people away,” Trump said. “Even Howard would say that.” Lutnick, sitting in the audience, quickly concurred. “We’ll take him.” By July, Huang was back in the Oval Office. His pitch this time was tailored to Trump. Selling chips to China, he argued, could create American jobs and cement American AI as the world standard. He had already said publicly in May that the ban already cost Nvidia $15 billion in sales. Two top administration officials who had become close Huang allies accompanied him in the Oval Office: Lutnick and David Sacks, the White House AI adviser, who championed “exporting the US AI stack” – the idea that selling older chips like the H20 abroad keeps the world hooked on American technology. Five days later, Nvidia announced the government had assured it that it would be permitted to sell the H20 in China. Huang was in Beijing when he said sales would resume. The next day, Lutnick went on CNBC, explaining the decision as a way to get China “addicted to the American technology stack.” The H20 deal was finished in August, and the president negotiated it himself, directly with Huang, as they sat face-to-face in the White House. Lutnick’s agency immediately moved to issue H20 licenses. Trump would go on to publicly confirm the arrangement that made the H20 sales possible: Nvidia would pay the government 15% of its China chip revenue. Through the fall, Huang drew closer to the president, and Trump regularly mentioned Huang off-the-cuff in his public remarks. In October, Trump spoke with Huang, Marc Benioff and other business leaders about sending federal law enforcement into San Francisco, and the next day he called the plan off, citing those conversations. That same month, as Trump was preparing to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping in South Korea, Nvidia donated $25 million to Trump’s White House ballroom project, a person familiar with the matter said. Nvidia never appeared on the published donor list. The warnings In the summer of 2025, as Trump and Huang were growing closer, a phone call began to unravel something larger. Singapore police, investigating a cloud company called Megaspeed, questioned its former managing director, Alice Huang, and barred her from leaving the country. She had met Jensen Huang at an Nvidia event in California in early 2024. The two were photographed together at a trade show in Taipei that June. During a briefing with lawmakers on Capitol Hill at the end of 2025, federal agents said they suspected Jensen Huang was the “target of a foreign intelligence effort,” citing his close relationship with Alice Huang, according to sources familiar with the meeting. The briefing was centered on an investigation into suspected efforts to circumvent US export control restrictions and attempts to influence the Trump administration’s policy on shipping certain Nvidia chips to China, according to the sources. The FBI, which is conducting the primary counterintelligence investigation, told lawmakers last year that it was particularly suspicious of Alice Huang’s seemingly overnight career pivot from Chinese State television journalist to businesswoman with an unusually large amount of purchasing power in the Chinese economy, one of the sources said. Trump himself had been briefed on intelligence about Alice Huang in late 2025 and took no action, CNN previously reported. But the investigations continued. The Commerce Department had been investigating Megaspeed since 2024 to determine whether the firm had run afoul of US export rules, but had stopped short of placing the company on the so-called Entity List, a trade blacklist that bars US suppliers from selling to listed firms without a license. Other areas of the administration had grown frustrated at the delay, including at the State Department and National Security Council, people familiar with the matter said. On Capitol Hill, Senate Intelligence Committee Chairman Tom Cotton, an Arkansas Republican, had taken notice and quickly fired off a direct request to Lutnick to investigate Megaspeed. Behind the scenes, executive branch officials from other national security agencies were raising Megaspeed as a clear target for investigation and inclusion on Commerce’s Entity List. They got no substantive response. And in meetings when the case came up, Lutnick’s deputies would respond by telling officials little more than it was Lutnick’s decision to make, according to people familiar with the conversations. In the CNBC interview Friday, Bessent suggested the inaction had violated directives given by Trump himself. “I am frustrated when President Trump made it very clear that China should not receive any Nvidia chips above H100s,” Bessent said, referring to an older-generation data-center chip. “And so any leakage is very frustrating because it hurts our great companies in the AI race, gives the Chinese an advantage.” When Trump was preparing to travel to China for a state visit in May, the delegation announced on May 11 initially didn’t include Huang. The next day, Trump phoned Huang to invite him. As Trump flew aboard Air Force One to Anchorage that afternoon with Elon Musk and Sean Hannity, he received a briefing from Secretary of State Marco Rubio about some of the concerns surrounding Huang and China. On the ground in Alaska, Huang boarded for the final leg to Beijing. On May 14, Xi greeted Trump at the Great Hall of the People, and Musk, Huang and Apple’s Tim Cook were the only executives the White House listed at the arrival ceremony. Huang called it “one of the most important summits in human history.” In the months that followed, there was little to indicate Trump or Lutnick had concerns about Huang. Trump praised him in the Oval Office. Lutnick, moderating a September G20 session in North Carolina, called him “an American treasure” — the same flattery deployed on their first phone call nearly two years earlier. In September, Huang took a call from Trump on stage and put him on speakerphone at a summit in Los Angeles. Trump called AI-takeover fears “a hoax,” called data centers “the oil of the next 20, 25 years,” and said opposition played into China’s hands. Ten days later, Huang and his wife were at the White House to attend Trump’s State Dinner for Chinese leader Xi Jinping. They were seated at the head table with the two leaders and their spouses. The reckoning Less than a month later, the first bombshell dropped: US officials had concluded Alice Huang was a Chinese intelligence asset who had cultivated a close relationship with Jensen Huang. CNN later reported the US intelligence community is still working to understand the relationship between Alice Huang and the Chinese government, with multiple sources telling CNN that the intelligence collected on her to date does not prove that she was acting as a spy for Beijing. Trump, officials said, would not hang his friend out to dry. As one official put it, Huang’s problems were Nvidia’s, Nvidia’s were the economy’s, and that became the president’s problem. Trump called Huang “brilliant” and, “unless we find out something to the contrary,” “very above board.” But the political ground had also shifted. Democrats won both chambers in the midterm elections, and voters rejected data-center projects in 40 of 41 ballot measures. The Republican chairs of three House committees – Foreign Affairs, Intelligence and the China select committee, all set to lose their gavels in January – asked Huang as well as Nvidia’s general counsel for closed-door interviews next month. Kessler, Lutnick’s deputy at the Commerce Department, has also been asked to appear at a hearing scheduled for next month. Republicans are now accusing Lutnick of putting Trump in a vulnerable position. “Shame on Lutnick for allowing that exposure to happen for the president. Raises a question about what other ones are out there,” Sen. Thom Tillis told reporters Thursday. During a meeting in the Situation Room last week, Treasury Secretary Bessent turned to Lutnick and asked why Megaspeed wasn’t on the entities list. According to sources familiar with the meeting, Lutnick stammered, “I don’t know. I’ll look into it.” This article has been updated with additional information.

articles.title: Small town residents cry for help as immigrant influx fueled by trucking industry has unintended consequences
articles.summary: A Fox News Digital investigation reveals Hamilton Township's freight fraud crackdown yielded 561 traffic stops and 36 arrests in southwest Ohio.
articles.body: This article is Part 3 of a Fox News Digital exclusive series investigating trucking fraud, public safety, and assimilation concerns in southwest Ohio. You can read Part 1 here and Part 2 here. OHIO - An influx of Uzbek immigrants and trucking companies, coupled with mounting concerns about roadway safety and alleged fraud, is fueling frustration in southwest Ohio, where residents are speaking out about changes they say have left them feeling unsafe on their roads and increasingly uneasy in their own neighborhoods. Jane, a resident of southwest Ohio, is one of many who have been affected by the Uzbek influx, which she says ultimately drove her out of a new home she purchased in the area after just 18 months of living there. "I have literally been screaming about what has been going on for years, and I'm like somebody needs to take notice of this," Jane told Fox News Digital. Jane recounted repeated problems involving neighbors she identified as Uzbek, describing unsupervised children grabbing moving cars, climbing construction equipment, threatening to punch, kick or choke her dog, and taking her child's bicycle while ignoring demands to return it. She also described children urinating on neighbors’ vehicles, adults slaughtering chickens outdoors in view of her frightened child, and semi-truck cabs obstructing driveways. WORKING-CLASS AMERICANS SAY THEIR TOWN IS THE NEXT DEARBORN — AND THEY'VE HAD ENOUGH Jane described feeling "incredibly uncomfortable" encountering groups of roughly 15 men she identified as Uzbek gathered on the grass between neighboring homes while she was walking her dog. "They all look at me like I have like 12 freaking heads, like I'm the most disgusting person in the world," she said. Jane also described a situation where a group of Uzbek men showed up at her neighbor's door late at night carrying large bags before being told by the neighbor they had the wrong address. That neighbor then watched them go across the street into a garage and count cash that came from inside those bags. She estimated calling police roughly 20 times or more and said she felt authorities were unwilling or unable to intervene, leaving her family feeling they had little recourse but to leave. Jane was granted anonymity and is not using her real name due to fear for her family’s safety and possible retribution. TRUMP ADMIN INVESTIGATING 75 TRUCK DRIVER SCHOOLS FOR FRAUD, HELPING NON-CITIZENS GET LICENSES In nearby Middletown, Fox News Digital visited a site in mid-October that used to be a restaurant where GHOSTOPSUZ, a resident who has been flagging suspicious trucking companies and Uzbek influx to his followers anonymously online, used to frequent every Sunday after Mass with his family as a child. Today, the building is abandoned and in disarray with smashed-out windows and no sign of life inside, but registered as the active headquarters of a trucking company, UAG Express, with over two dozen violations for infractions including vehicle maintenance, unsafe driving, suspended-CDL and an hours-of-service violation. "It's devastating, dude, I mean, it really is," GHOSTOPSUZ said as he walked around the dilapidated building that had multiple big rigs parked in the back but no sign of any recent activity. The location was recently highlighted by Border Hawk News. "My daughter plays competitive volleyball, so we're on these roads that we're sharing with these people that don't speak English, don't understand our laws, can't read our laws and frankly, I don't think they care, it’s quite obvious…and it doesn’t show respect for the community that you're in to do things like this." OUT OF CONTROL, UNQUALIFIED ILLEGAL ALIEN TRUCKERS ENDANGERING KIDS ON US ROADS, INSIDER WARNS: ‘JUST MADNESS’ Fox News Digital reached out to UAG Express, owned by Aziz Ishanov, for comment but did not receive a response. On Nov. 4, Fox News Digital attended a meeting where dozens of Hamilton Township residents expressed their concerns to the local trustees and told stories of first-hand experiences ranging from alleged trucking fraud to the mosque, to crowded schools, to crime concerns related to the Uzbek community in the area. "It has been a great place to grow up, now I'm very concerned at this point with what we're learning about the fraud from these trucking companies, the Uzbek trucking companies, about the funds that they're using to build the mosque right now. I'm just wondering, how did this get approved in the first place?" One local resident asked. Residents voiced concerns about a wide variety of issues including Uzbek men leering at women outside gyms, crowded schools, an unsupervised Uzbek child who recently drowned in a local pond, and Uzbek truck drivers offering money to women to get inside their trucks. One resident said, "Christian values are not compatible with Islamic values; they just simply aren't, and I don't like calling a people group out, especially as a Christian, that's very hard for me to do. But the facts are the facts, and we have to look at the facts. They are not here to assimilate; some are, I'm sure. But I know how they operate." "We are drowning," one resident said while discussing the crowded schools and students who can't speak English which has stretched resources thin. "We are drowning here, our kids our suffering." Local law enforcement has taken action on the trucking safety issue, and in the meeting, Hamilton Township Police Chief Quillan Short unveiled the data from a recent freight fraud crackdown that multiple local agencies coordinated between Oct. 19-23. That operation resulted in 561 traffic stops, 258 truck inspections, 423 citations and 73 vehicles being placed out of service. Authorities also placed 49 drivers out of service and made 36 arrests, including 31 on charges related to immigration-related offenses, according to data presented by Short. Hamilton Township Trustee Darryl Cordrey, in a statement to Fox News Digital, called the results of the crackdown "staggering" especially considering it only lasted 5 days. "Hamilton Township residents have every right to be concerned about unsafe commercial vehicles , unqualified drivers on our roads, and other criminal issues that have stemmed from the substantial increase in commercial trucking operations in Hamilton Township," Cordrey said. "Our residents should not have to bear the consequences of failures in immigration policy and commercial trucking oversight." Cordrey added that the Biden administration's immigration policies have "contributed to the broader problems we are now confronting" and that he is "fully committed" to doing his part to resolve the issues working alongside local, state, and federal agencies. Ohio Republican state lawmaker Michelle Teska was present at the meeting as well and has taken action on the issue in the form of a bill to strengthen commercial-driver licensing requirements, including a measure requiring driver examinations to be administered in English. "We have a community that's being inundated with people from a certain area and how they got here is through the trucking industry, and they got here because, again, in the state of Ohio, you can get a CDL and a driver's license in 10 different languages," Teska told Fox News Digital, adding that she and the Hamilton Township trustees share the frustration and are doing what they can to address it despite many of the issues being rooted at the state and federal level. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The federal government has ramped up efforts to crack down on trucking fraud over the past year, and the Department of Transportation and Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration have mounted a sweeping crackdown on fraud and safety violations, placing roughly 34,000 drivers out of service for failing basic English-language proficiency requirements, revoking or canceling more than 31,000 illegally issued commercial driver’s licenses, and shutting down or purging nearly 10,000 noncompliant driving schools from the federal registry. "This is a safety issue," Teska said. "This is not a partisan issue in any way, shape, or form, but this is a safety issue, and you know we've had a rape conviction, a federal human smuggling indictment, a fatal crash where a driver couldn't communicate with troopers without a translator, and every single one of those things was preventable." Warren County Prosecutor David Fornshell previously told Fox News Digital that clearly "there’s something going on" within the Uzbek community in southwest Ohio that "warrants at least awareness on the part of law enforcement." "I would say hardly a week goes by where we don't have some felony case involving an Uzbek, it's pretty frequent at this point," Fornshell said. On Friday, the Islamic Center of Maineville, the mosque that has drawn the ire of some in the community, posted on its Telegram channel that it acknowledges the concerns and is hoping to work with the community to resolve them. "On behalf of the Hamkor Uzbek Cincinnati Association, we recognize that some local residents have concerns and questions about our community. We believe that mutual respect, open communication, and understanding are the best ways to address these issues," the message said. "Our Uzbek community is willing to listen to local residents, understand their concerns, clear up any misunderstandings, and work together to find practical solutions. We want to build trust, strengthen relationships, and promote unity between the Uzbek community and our neighbors. We believe that respectful dialogue and cooperation, rather than arguments and division, will help us move forward as one community." Data from the 2024 Census show that roughly 1,500 people born in Uzbekistan live in Greater Cincinnati, while about 3,800 Uzbekistan-born residents live across Ohio. Uzbek community leaders say the actual population is significantly higher, estimating that roughly 4,000 Uzbek families live in southern Ohio, including U.S.-born children. "Our community was selected by the Uzbeks because they didn't think we would push back on their foreign influence," online researcher Nodawolf, a local resident who has been at the forefront of reporting on alleged trucking fraud over the past year, said via a statement read by an attendee at the trustees meeting. "Here we are. We are here to say that our community will not be exploited for their monetary gain." America Up Close is a Fox News Digital Politics series taking the country’s biggest political debates beyond Washington to uncover their real-world costs for the Americans living with the results.

articles.title: Democrats bullish on South after historic midterms gains
articles.summary: Democrats are seeing new opportunities in the South after stunning midterm victories in Mississippi, South Carolina and Texas. The party’s wins were both big and broad: It flipped highly competitive Senate seats in North Carolina, South Carolina, Texas and Mississippi, delivered new Democratic governors in the Lone Star State and Georgia, and took control of…
articles.body:
Democrats are seeing new opportunities in the South after stunning midterm victories in Mississippi, South Carolina and Texas .

The party’s wins were both big and broad: It flipped highly competitive Senate seats in North Carolina, South Carolina, Texas and Mississippi, delivered new Democratic governors in the Lone Star State and Georgia, and took control of the state Houses in Texas, Georgia and North Carolina.

Now, Democrats in the South are calling on their party to rethink their approach and invest more heavily in the region’s voting blocs ahead of the 2028 presidential election.

“The South is not just winnable; it also completely changes the calculus of the path of victory for the presidency if any Southern states are in play,” said Fred Hicks, a Democratic strategist based in Georgia and Florida.

“I think Democrats need to take a page from Republicans’ 2024 strategy where they decided to try to penetrate the blue wall, and I think we need to look at that with the red wall,” Hicks added. “We should not cede anything in the South.”

After a string of blue wins in the South and days of suspense in a razor-tight race, Democrat Scott Colom this week flipped the Senate seat in Mississippi for the first time in decades — the latest signal, party operatives argue, that Democrats shouldn’t count out the South.

Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, a rare Democrat to lead a deep-red state, said on the social platform X that “for too long, Southern Democrats have been overlooked, left out, and even looked down upon” — but that, in the wake of Colom’s win, they’re “on the rise.”

“In the past, the party would invest in places like Mississippi just enough to force the Republicans to spend money. Same thing in Texas, same thing in South Carolina, same thing in Georgia. Until we began to win,” Sen. Raphael Warnock (D-Ga.) told The Washington Sun .

Colom argued on X that prognosticators’ label on the Senate race as “solid R” made it more difficult to fundraise “and are part of the reason the South has been neglected for so long.” He told MS NOW his success “proves that the future of the party has to include the South.”

National Democrats were eyeing openings in the South early in the midterms. The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC) expanded its battleground with a focus on Florida, Georgia and Texas this summer, and the Democratic National Committee (DNC) launched a Southern States Resource Hub investment in August as Chair Ken Martin announced “the puck is heading to the South.”

Top groups didn’t start serious spending in Mississippi, though, until October. The Democrats’ Senate campaign arm jumped in with $500,000 just days before the election — which ended up, nationally, as the most expensive midterms on record .

Florida Senate candidate Angie Nixon (D), who narrowly lost to Republican incumbent Sen. Ashley Moody, has also criticized her party for being “gun-shy” about backing Democrats in the South, particularly Black women, and called her race a “missed opportunity.”

Though she got support from Martin, Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) and other top Democrats, Nixon suggested on “The Don Lemon Show” that the money came too late in the game to get her over the finish line.

Democrats have long concentrated much of their campaign efforts on swing states and shoring up the “blue wall” across the Midwest and the Rust Belt, but the upsets and close races in the South this cycle expand the party’s House and Senate map — and could open up doors in the next presidential race.

“That’s the message going forward: The South has something to say,” said Antjuan Seawright, a Democratic strategist based in South Carolina, describing “a tectonic plate shift all across the South.”

The Palmetto State elected Democrat Annie Andrews in a surprise upset over Republican Sen. Darline Graham (S.C.), whom President Trump personally picked to succeed her late brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.). She’s South Carolina’s first Democratic senator in almost three decades.

Driving blue wins in South Carolina and beyond were Black voters, who have long favored Democrats but shifted to the right in the last presidential election. Amid poor approval ratings for President Trump and Republican-led redistricting efforts that critics panned as diluting Black political power, the bloc turned out in big numbers to boost Democrats.

Party strategists say the newly elected Democrats now need to deliver on their campaign promises and keep Black voters at the fore to prevent a reversal in 2028.

“Let’s start with who makes up the South, and that’s Black voters and rural voters,” Seawright said of his party’s next moves. “We have to treat the South and … the coalitions that make up the Southern coalition, as a long-term investment, not an expense.”

Democrats also hit historic milestones with their Southern wins. Along with first-in-decades flips from red to blue, Colom will be Mississippi’s first Black senator in more than a century and Georgia Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms will be the country’s first Black woman to serve as governor. In Texas, Democrat Gina Hinojosa was elected as the state’s first Hispanic woman in the governor’s mansion.

“To have Georgia, which was once the headquarters of the Confederacy, elect a Black woman governor, I think it just shows that Black voters understood the assignment and where they were currently in history, and decided to act upon it,” said Douglas Wilson, a Democratic strategist based in North Carolina.

Republicans notched a historic win of their own in the region with Rep. Byron Donalds (R-Fla.), who won the Florida race to become the Sunshine State’s first Black governor — but Democrats see his 1-point lead over Democrat David Jolly as yet another sign of blue inroads.

“What it has looked like in the past … we have to almost prove to the national party, ‘Hey, we can win this,’ and that process usually takes six months to a year,” Wilson said.

“What needs to happen going forward is that the DNC right now needs to start placing boots on the ground a year or two out from 2028 to focus on organizing precincts, recruiting volunteers, and helping the state party with any resources that they need,” he said, adding that the party “cannot wait until the summer of 2028” to get started.

The DNC has said it’s locked in on just that.

“This midterm election’s results in the South proved our theory of the case: that when you invest and organize everywhere, you can win anywhere. Democrats are on offense in the South,” DNC spokesperson Angelo Fernández Hernández said in a statement.

“We will continue to invest in the South and double down on our proven work to win in 2028 and beyond.”

The Democrats’ presidential nominating calendar will kick off 2028 in South Carolina , after a push to feature more diverse voices in the early votes put the Palmetto State ahead of New Hampshire and Iowa, which have long held the first-in-the-nation primary and caucus.

Hicks also argued that Georgia will be “the new Iowa” for Democrats seeking the party’s White House nod.

And several of the party’s potential 2028 contenders hail from the South: from Kentucky’s Beshear, who said he’s open to the idea , to Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff (D), who’s denied the speculation and just won a second term. Georgia’s other senator, Warnock, is up for reelection in 2028 but could also mount a presidential bid.

In the meantime, Democrats will have new opportunities to test their momentum next year with off-cycle races for governor and other offices in five states, including Louisiana, Kentucky and Mississippi.

Investing in those states — and throughout the South — in 2027 “will yield dividends in 2028,” Hicks said.

“We have proven time and time again that winning at the local level is key to building credibility up the ballot,” said Miami Mayor Eileen Higgins, who won an off-year 2025 race to become the city’s first female leader and the first Democratic mayor since 1997.

Going into 2028, Higgins predicted that national Democrats will also rethink their approach to places like Florida “now that we have Democratic governors and Democratic senators all throughout the South” because they’ve proven they can win “with no investment, with just the infrastructure we built on the ground and the quality of candidates we have.”

articles.title: Confirming judges, defense funding top of GOP’s lame-duck agenda: Cramer
articles.summary: Sen. Kevin Cramer (R-N.D.) said he and his fellow GOP senators will focus on confirming President Trump’s federal judge nominees during their remaining time leading the upper chamber, laying out the Republican Party’s lame duck agenda in an interview Sunday. “What we need to do is make sure that every nominee for a lifetime judgeship,…
articles.body:
Sen. Kevin Cramer (R-N.D.) said he and his fellow GOP senators will focus on confirming President Trump’s federal judge nominees during their remaining time leading the upper chamber, laying out the Republican Party’s lame duck agenda in an interview Sunday.

“What we need to do is make sure that every nominee for a lifetime judgeship, either on the federal district court, or more importantly, even the circuit courts of appeals, we need to get them confirmed,” Cramer said in an interview on “ The Cats Roundtable with John Catsimatidis ” radio show.

On Thursday, the Senate voted to confirm judicial nominee Gregory Carl Cook to serve on a U.S. d istrict c ourt in Alabama and moved forward another judicial nominee for a circuit court .

Cramer, who formerly chaired the North Carolina Republican Party, expressed optimism the Senate could “take up another batch of judges” this week.

“That’s really our top priority as conservatives,” he said, adding, “It’s Donald Trump’s top priority.”

Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) has made confirming the Trump administration’s federal judge nominees a top issue for Republicans in the lame duck session, even added extra legislative days this week to confirm judicial appointments.

“Before the end of the year, Senate Republicans will prioritize confirming President Trump’s team and his nominees to the federal judiciary,” Thune wrote in a Tuesday post to social platform X.

Following Cook’s Thursday confirmation, the number of confirmed federal judges by the 119th Congress rose to 58, according to the Administrative Office of the U.S. Courts .

Thune touted these numbers in a social media post that afternoon.

“[The Senate GOP] has spent the last two years confirming President Trump’s lifetime federal judges at the fastest pace – from nomination to confirmation – since Reagan was in office,” the majority leader wrote, adding, “Our work will have a generational effect.”

In addition to federal judges, Cramer also emphasized a focus on confirming executive cabinet positions.

“There are a whole bunch of other professional staff or professional political staff, undersecretaries, deputy secretaries, things like that,” he said. “So those we can all do with just 50 votes or more.”

The North Dakota Republican also advocated for passing a budget reconciliation package during the lame duck session. Trump has urged the Senate to allocate $350 billion for national defense.

“I think there’s a very good chance we can do that,” Cramer said, noting the support for this effort from House Minority Leader-designate Jim Jordan (R-Ohio).

“The reason that’s so important is because what’s going to happen for the next two years,” the senator said. “They’re going to — the Democrats — are going to do what they always do. They’re going to gut national defense.”

Democrats in the House and Senate have approved war powers resolutions, with the support of several Republicans, to urge the Trump administration to end its military operations against Iran.

Additionally, progressive lawmakers have vowed to bring impeachment proceedings against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth in the next Congress, after the House failed to advance an effort to oust the Pentagon chief this past week.

articles.title: Inside Senate GOP's tense post-election reckoning as Thune clashes with Republican critics
articles.summary: Senate Republicans kept John Thune as leader by acclamation after a heated closed-door meeting that some lawmakers compared to "Festivus."
articles.body: Senate Republicans huddled for hours on end to define their remaining time in power and determine if the leadership they had backed so far was the right choice moving forward into a new era in Washington, D.C. Some closed-door meetings over the last nearly two years Republicans have controlled the Senate have been animated, with policy pitches devolving into shouting matches — President Donald Trump and Sen. Bill Cassidy, R-La., infamously sparred over the Iran war earlier this year. This confab, their first since Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., and Democrats roared back into the majority, was different. In part, it was meant to develop a plan that would carry them through the final weeks of this year — that was agreed upon during the meeting, but not without its own drama after the fact on who could lay claim to the GOP’s 54-day blitz. SENATE GOP REBELLION FIZZLES AS THUNE KEEPS POWER DESPITE HISTORIC MIDTERM MASSACRE It was also a test to see if Republicans wanted to keep Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., as their leader, or delay until a challenger appeared. But Republicans pushing for a delay acknowledged part of the problem: Who would want the job? "I got the job because nobody else wants it," Thune told Fox News Digital after the dust settled in the Old Senate Chamber. And he did, along with much of the same leadership team that Senate Republicans elected when they won the majority two years ago, by acclamation, meaning no lawmaker objected to their leadership slate. Some told Fox News Digital it was like "Festivus," the holiday etched into Gen-Xers' brains from "Seinfeld" known for its airing of grievances. Others described it as a frank, needed debrief as the GOP picks through the debris of Election Night. GOP SENATOR WITHHOLDS SUPPORT FOR THUNE AS LEADERSHIP SHOWDOWN LOOMS "It really was, to be honest with you, as profound as the loss was last week. I would have expected more emotions, which I consider to be a good sign," Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., told Fox News Digital. "But I think it's almost — It's self-governing because nobody can dispute that it's a problem." "Now it's not like you're looking for the silver lining," he continued. "It doesn't exist. It is what it is, and you've got to react." But there were some "testy" moments, particularly between Thune and Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., the driving force behind the push to delay leadership elections. For Thune, the main question was what anyone else in the Senate GOP would have done differently in his shoes. "I just think that you come through an election like this and everybody's looking for scapegoats and there's a lot of blame casting that goes on, and I just wanted to get up and basically defend what we had done and accomplished," Thune said. "And I think the operative question is, tell me what you would do differently? Both on the political side and the legislative side. So we had a good, we had a robust conversation, and it does. It always gets a little bit testy in the back and forth, but I thought that, by and large, the discussion was very candid, and certainly gave everybody an opportunity to be heard." CONGRESS RETURNS TO BRUTAL LAME-DUCK STRETCH WITH SHUTDOWN DEADLINE, LEADERSHIP RACES: 'CLOSET IS FULL OF S—' Johnson acknowledged that he was "prone to interrupting, I’m rude that way," and told Fox News Digital that he was sure Thune was "not happy that I did that," but assured that there was no "animus" between the two. "In politics, everything has to be so black and white, and, unfortunately, for our base, the way to really rev them up is inter-conference fighting, which is not helpful," Johnson said. "So, again, I didn't really like doing this, but it had to be done," he continued. "I mean, we had to, and in the end, I think, resulted in a very, very good conversation and pretty well revealed we're just lucky to have anybody who wants those jobs." Sen. Steve Daines, R-Mont., told Fox News Digital that Thune showed "moments of exceptional leadership" in the heat of the meeting. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP He noted that the top Republican's rebuttal reminded lawmakers of the "ebb and flow of the politics in our country," dating back to 1986, when former President Ronald Reagan, then entering his final midterm election similar to Trump, lost eight seats in the upper chamber. "Obama lost nine Senate seats in 2014, it looks like we're going to lose eight, depending on what happens in Alaska," Daines said. "So it's within the kind of the historic norms of going back and forth." "And the leader forcefully laid that out and then talked about what he needed to do going forward to unify and eventually reclaim the majority," he continued.

articles.title: How lower courts became the last line of defense for the 2026 elections
articles.summary: Democrats need to use their new majority in Congress to address partisan gerrymandering, strengthen the Voting Rights Act, and regulate the flood of dark money into politics, even if some reforms may not be possible until a new president is elected or new justices join the Supreme Court.
articles.body:
In less than two decades, the U.S. Supreme Court has rendered elections far less likely to reflect the will of the people. Yet when President Trump tried to put both thumbs on the scale of the 2026 midterms, federal judges repeatedly stood in his way.

In Citizens United v. Federal Election Commission , the court in 2010 ruled that corporations and unions have a First Amendment right to spend unlimited amounts on independent political ads. Although the decision affirmed public disclosure laws, loopholes have enabled wealthy donors and organizations to funnel massive amounts of money into political contests through entities that don’t disclose contributors’ names.

Nine years later, in Rucho v. Common Cause , the court declared that federal judges have no ability to stop partisan gerrymandering by the states, while acknowledging it might be “incompatible with democratic principles.”

And in this year’s Louisiana v. Callais decision, the court largely gutted a provision of the Voting Rights Act that prevented state legislatures from using racially discriminatory political maps in redistricting.

Emboldened, no doubt, by these decisions, Trump has ignored the provision in the U.S. Constitution, which authorizes the states — not the president — to set the time, place and manner of elections, subject to laws enacted by Congress, and has repeatedly sought to impose federal control over voter registration, ballot distribution, and vote counting.

He has been thwarted at least 34 times by federal judges appointed by both Democratic and Republican presidents, including his own. And Trump’s Department of Justice is zero for 28 in lawsuits demanding that states provide complete voter rolls to the federal government, which critics believe the administration intended to use to compile its own list of eligible voters.

In League of Women Voters of Massachusetts v. Trump , a federal court in September blocked the U.S. Postal Service from implementing Trump’s executive order directing it to refuse to deliver ballots to individuals who did not appear on newly created federal voter eligibility rolls. The court found the order, which could have disenfranchised millions of American citizens, an unconstitutional intrusion on state authority over elections.

In October, the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals upheld a lower court ruling blocking a Trump administration demand that California set aside roughly 20,000 ballots cast by voters whose citizenship the Justice Department said it doubted. The judges found unconvincing the department’s allegations that some or all of them were not qualified to vote. Nor were the judges persuaded that the ballots could be sequestered “without potentially catastrophic effects on the entire system.” On Nov. 2, the day before the midterm elections were held, the Supreme Court declined to intervene , leaving the Ninth Circuit decision in place.

In at least one case, however, the lower courts did not respond well. After a federal district court in Northern California temporarily blocked the administration from threatening to prosecute election workers who did not comply with directions about handling ballots, a divided Ninth Circuit stayed that order . Dissenting judges warned that election workers would face “an impossible dilemma” because following state election laws might expose them to federal prosecution.

In most cases, however, lower courts held firm.

On Nov. 1, a federal judge dismissed a lawsuit seeking to preemptively challenge the U.S. Senate election in Alaska. The Department of Justice argued that Democrats had recruited Daniel J. Sullivan to run in an effort to draw votes from the Republican candidate, Daniel S. Sullivan. Noting that the state Division of Elections had already addressed the issue by requiring language on the ballot that would differentiate between the two candidates, the U.S. District Court for Alaska declared there was “no workable plan” to segregate the challenged ballots and that doing so would “clearly violate Alaskans’ right to a secret ballot.”

In several decisions, judges could not be clearer about the significance of federal intervention in elections. As the U.S. District Court for the Central District of California warned this year in U.S. v. Weber , “the taking of democracy does not occur in one fell swoop; it is chipped away piece-by-piece until there is nothing left.”

The Constitution states, unequivocally, that only states and Congress have the power to regulate elections . The executive branch may enforce election laws but cannot override them. Federal judges enforced that distinction when it mattered most. Those judges deserve our gratitude.

But democracy should not depend on the willingness of individual judges to resist presidential pressure based on unfounded allegations of fraud. Democrats need to use their new majority in Congress to address partisan gerrymandering, strengthen the Voting Rights Act, and regulate the flood of dark money into politics, even if some reforms may not be possible until a new president is elected or new justices join the Supreme Court.

For now, it helps to know that our institutions have held, if just barely.

David Wippman is emeritus president of Hamilton College. Glenn C. Altschuler is the Thomas and Dorothy Litwin Emeritus Professor of American Studies at Cornell University.

articles.title: Trump's top officials retreat behind military gates as ex-FBI deputy points to what's fueling threats
articles.summary: Scott Bessent joins Todd Blanche, Marco Rubio and Pete Hegseth at Washington D.C. military bases amid Iranian assassination threats.
articles.body: Military bases around Washington, D.C., have become an increasingly common refuge for some of President Donald Trump's most powerful officials, as threats linked to Iran and a surge in threats against public officials raise security concerns across the administration. "So you have this combination of a permission structure on the left for violence, combine it with the ability to track it and create a long paper trail, and the numbers explode, and these threat matrices go crazy," former Secret Service agent and former FBI Deputy Director Dan Bongino said. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is the latest senior administration official to relocate to a military installation, joining a growing number of top Trump officials living behind military gates as federal authorities confront security threats that extend well beyond the White House. IRAN HAS 'SUBSTANTIALLY INCREASED' EFFORTS TO TARGET AMERICANS ABROAD, US INTELLIGENCE MEMO WARNS "After The Wall Street Journal published an article featuring an online photo that allowed the location of the Secretary’s Georgetown home to be geo-located, security concerns began to increase which have now forced the Secretary to relocate to a military base for his safety. The news media has an obligation to act responsibly amid growing threats against public officials," a source familiar with the situation told Fox News Digital. Threats against Bessent had reached "more than an advanced stage" amid reported Iranian assassination threats, a senior administration official told Fox News Digital on Tuesday, but did not elaborate. The Iranian threats against Bessent come amid a documented history of alleged Tehran-backed assassination plots targeting senior U.S. officials. Attorney General Todd Blanche also relocated to a military base from his home around March, a different source familiar with the arrangements told Fox News Digital on Thursday. The Justice Department charged a member of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps in 2022 in an alleged murder-for-hire plot targeting former Trump national security adviser John Bolton, while prosecutors disclosed in 2024 that another Iranian operative had allegedly been tasked with developing a plan to assassinate Trump. Bongino said federal protection decisions are generally driven by threat assessments that account for threatening communications, social media activity and intelligence gathered by security personnel. Agencies responsible for protecting senior officials use those assessments to determine what level of protection is necessary. Secret Service Director Sean Curran said last month that threats against the agency's full-time protectees had increased more than 40% from the previous year, with roughly 10,000 threat cases recorded in 2026 at the time. Fox News Digital reached out to the White House and Secret Service for comment. "Pretty much, sadly, anyone at the cabinet, or even sub-cabinet level, with any kind of public persona in the Trump administration, needed a detail," Bongino said. US EVACUATES 13 MILITARY AIRCRAFT FROM SECOND UK BASE AS NEW IRAN THREAT RAISES ALARM The assassination of conservative activist Charlie Kirk and multiple attempts on President Donald Trump's life have heightened concerns about political violence, as security officials confront a growing volume of threats against public officials. Bongino pointed to his own experience as FBI deputy director, saying his security needs were comparable to those of some of the government's highest-ranking law enforcement officials. "Mine was on par with the attorney general and the FBI director that we had to expand it," Bongino said of his threat assessment and security detail. "It was an independent analysis." Bongino said social media has made threats against public officials easier to track, but the sheer volume of online activity has also created more work for investigators trying to determine which threats are credible. SECRET SERVICE CHIEF SAYS THREATS AGAINST PROTECTEES UP 40%, CITES INTERNET AND MENTAL HEALTH Bongino said the disruption to Bessent's personal life underscores the seriousness of the security concerns surrounding his move. "For him to have to uproot his life. And move on to a military facility where the housing's not terrible in those places, but it's certainly not what he's used to," Bongino said. "This stuff, it's not a convenience issue, I can promise you that. This is definitely serious stuff." Lawmakers have also raised concerns about security and federal spending. Rep. George Whitesides, D-Calif., secured House Armed Services Committee approval in June for a proposal seeking a Pentagon report on political appointees living in military housing, including the threats justifying their moves, legal authority for the arrangements and rental costs. Sen. Maggie Hassan, D-N.H., also questioned whether the reported transfer of $415 million in Secret Service funding to White House construction projects could affect the agency's protective operations, citing federal watchdog concerns about staffing and resource shortages. Barry Donadio, a former Secret Service agent who served during the George W. Bush and Barack Obama administrations, similarly told Fox News Digital that the decision to relocate Bessent to a military installation suggests an extraordinary level of concern among those responsible for his protection. "My first inkling is that the [threat] is so high that they cannot protect him with certainty, unless he is on a military base which speaks volumes for the situation at hand," Donadio said. TRUMP ADMIN APPROVES $351 MILLION FOR WHITE HOUSE SECURITY MEASURES AMID QUESTIONS OVER BALLROOM FUNDING Donadio said the move could indicate that officials believe Bessent would be safer on a military base than at a private residence. "They may have foiled an attack already that is not being publicized, and as an extra measure, have moved him to a military base for protective custody," Donadio said, clarifying that he did not mean Bessent was in custody, but rather under heightened government protection. Bessent is not the only senior Trump administration official whose security concerns have prompted a move to military housing. Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Secretary of War Pete Hegseth have reportedly taken up residence at Fort McNair in Washington, D.C., while White House chief of staff Stephen Miller and other administration officials have moved to military installations or protected government housing. TRUMP ADMIN APPROVES $351 MILLION FOR WHITE HOUSE SECURITY MEASURES AMID QUESTIONS OVER BALLROOM FUNDING The relocations have not all stemmed from the same threats. Some followed concerns about domestic political violence, while Bessent's move comes amid reported threats linked to Iran. Bongino said threats against high-profile officials can also extend beyond their time in government, describing an incident in which an individual allegedly appeared at a California television studio with a manifesto threatening him and other officials. "I mean, this stuff is real, it happens every day," Bongino said. "And when you're living through it and you're not accustomed to it, you know, and it follows you after office too." He said officials including Bessent, FBI Director Kash Patel, CIA Director John Ratcliffe and Hegseth understood that public service in the administration could make them targets even after leaving office. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Fort McNair, a historic Army installation along the Potomac River in Washington, D.C., has emerged as one of the military properties housing senior Trump administration officials. The installation, which dates to the late 1700s, is home to the National Defense University and traditionally provides residential quarters for senior military leaders. Fort McNair's residential quarters are divided into two housing groups, according to a 2020 National Capital Planning Commission report, while a 2024 Army filing identifies 27 historic homes built before 1919 at the installation. The Army's housing website lists 88 historic dwelling units across Fort McNair and nearby Fort Myer combined, without specifying how many are at each base. The growing use of military housing by senior civilian officials also raises questions about who approves the arrangements, whether officials pay for their accommodations and what impact, if any, the moves have on housing traditionally reserved for military personnel.

articles.title: Ayuso vuelve a cargar contra Begoña Gómez en Móstoles: "Lo único que tenía que haber hecho es echarme un novio socialista"
articles.standfirst: La presidenta madrileña ironiza con el "ascenso meteórico" de la mujer de Pedro Sánchez
articles.summary: La presidenta madrileña ironiza con el "ascenso meteórico" de la mujer de Pedro Sánchez
articles.body: La presidenta de la Comunidad de Madrid y del PP madrileño, Isabel Díaz Ayuso, ha vuelto a cargar este domingo contra Begoña Gómez, esposa del presidente del Gobierno, Pedro Sánchez, durante un mitin de campaña en Móstoles de cara a las elecciones generales del 29 de noviembre. Ante los simpatizantes, y con el lema "El cambio necesario" en el atril, Ayuso se refirió a "la mujer del presidente, que ahora también es mitinera", después de que Gómez apareciera en un acto socialista en Sevilla. "Por tanto, si te expones... si no sabes torear, Manolete, ¿para qué te metes? Si te metes en campaña, te metes en campaña", advirtió. La dirigente popular ironizó después sobre la trayectoria profesional de Gómez, a la que acusó de dar "lecciones de feminismo": "Digo, fíjate la que ha ascendido tan lejos por sus propios méritos. No hay más que ver el ascenso meteórico laboral que ha tenido". Y lo comparó con su propio caso: "Me tengo que poner a pensar y digo yo: ¿para qué estudié durante estos años previos? ¿Para qué hice la selectividad? ¿Para qué curré para poder llegar a la universidad pública, si lo único que tenía que haber hecho es echarme un novio?". "Pero cómo no me di cuenta, es que en esta vida se vive mucho mejor siendo socialista", continuó, "porque como no es el talento, no es tu creatividad, no es lo que tú aportas lo que se mide, sino lo que te prestas al líder y a la causa". "Pues a lo mejor, oye, algunos se han equivocado", remató. En el mismo acto, Ayuso volvió a recurrir a la metáfora de las garrapatas, que ya había empleado días antes en un mitin en Torrejón de Ardoz. “Hay que quitar a la garrapata y los que somos de pueblo sabemos cómo hacerlo: quitarle la cabeza y con aceite. Con los votos, malpensados. Hay que ir a votar. También se puede extirpar de manera quirúrgica. Pero eso ya para otro momento”, ha dicho entre bromas Ayuso. “El garrapatismo es vivir de lo público para que lo público no funcione. Como dice el presidente colombiano Gustavo Petro: ‘Hay que hacer que la gente sea pobre porque sino deja de votar a la izquierda’”, ha añadido en su discurso la presidenta de la Comunidad de Madrid. Ayuso cerró filas en el Teatro del Bosque con el alcalde de Móstoles, Manuel Bautista, a quien un juzgado de violencia sobre la mujer investiga desde julio por presunto acoso sexual y laboral tras la querella de una exconcejala del PP. La presidenta acusó a Moncloa de orquestar una campaña de desprestigio contra el regidor y le vaticinó la mayoría absoluta: "Vas a tener una mayoría absoluta gracias al acoso, a la mentira, al desprestigio y a tu trabajo". "Yo sé que la mafia ha llamado a tu puerta", le dijo, antes de rechazar lo que llamó "técnicas chavistas": "Conmigo no van". Sobre la causa judicial, sostuvo que "lo que diga un juez cuando decida eso es otro tema, pero ya estás desprestigiado". Bautista niega los hechos y ha descartado dimitir.

articles.title: Bessent, Congress zero in on Lutnick’s role in Nvidia-Megaspeed scandal
articles.summary: Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick is facing heat in Washington, including from Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, over his approach to AI chip export controls...
articles.body:
Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick is facing heat in Washington, including from Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, over his approach to AI chip export controls amid Nvidia's national security scandal.

Reports emerged this week that Lutnick took a softer line on Nvidia over the tech giant's AI chip sales to China and failed to put the Singaporean firm Megaspeed on the trade entity blacklist.

Following bipartisan calls to testify, Lutnick has agreed to appear before Congress, but the blame game is already starting with the Trump administration.

"Treasury, War, USTR [U.S. Trade Representative] and State … were in favor of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months," Bessent said Friday on CNBC's "Squawk Box."

"But Commerce has the pen. Commerce BIS has the pen, and you will have to ask them about their internal processes," Bessent added, referring to Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security.

Axios reported Bessent confronted Lutnick last week about the failure to put Megaspeed on Commerce's entity list , a directory of companies that pose national security risks.

Lutnick said he would "look into it," while Axios reported the Commerce secretary has been circumventing other administration officials who have sought to tighten the screws on Megaspeed due to its link to China.

Megaspeed is at the center of the Nvidia scandal, an ordeal that led the company's founder, Jensen Huang, to resign as CEO on Thursday .

Huang admitted last week he had an extramarital affair, and reports indicate it was with Alice Huang, formerly a Megaspeed executive and a woman whom U.S. intelligence officials believe may be a Chinese spy, the New York Times (NYT) reported on Oct. 29.

It is not clear when President Trump, Lutnick or other Commerce officials were informed of the U.S. intelligence community's suspicions, but Bessent's comments signal the administration was aware of risks involving Megaspeed.

During his CNBC interview on Friday, Bessent said he and Deputy Treasury Secretary Francis Brooke have "been pushing" for Commerce to add Megaspeed to the entity list "for months."

"This is a BIS decision," Bessent noted, after dismissing host Joe Kernen's suggestion that the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control could take action.

Lawmakers on Capitol Hill are launching probes into the matter and, given Lutnick's role, sought the Cabinet official's testimony. The Commerce secretary agreed to appear before the Senate Banking Committee, chaired by Sen. Tim Scott (R-S.C.), on Dec. 10.

"Recent developments underscore the significant national security and economic interests at stake and the need for timely, substantive engagement with Congress," Scott wrote in a letter he sent to Lutnick on Thursday.

Democratic Sen. Chris Coons (D-Del.) cast Lutnick in sharper terms, writing Thursday on the social platform X the Commerce secretary "let the American people down" and put the country's national security "at risk" by allowing Megaspeed to receive advanced AI chips from Nvidia.

"Lutnick has a lot to answer to," added Coons, a member of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee who is poised to chair the panel once Democrats take the majority.

Marshall Billingslea, who worked at the Treasury Department during Trump's first term, noted it is "quite unusual" for Bessent to go public about Cabinet-level discussions about "a matter as sensitive as" the Nvidia-Megaspeed affair.

"To his credit, Scott Bessent & [Secretary of State Marco] Rubio's team have consistently been right on this topic. Lutnick just ran roughshod over everyone," Billingslea, the former assistant Treasury secretary for terrorist financing, wrote on X .

He speculated, "I wonder if this means the Commerce Secretary is on his way out?"

In a research note Friday, Beacon Policy Advisors suggested "Lutnick could take the fall, or the administration could push out a lower-ranking official instead" like BIS head Jeffrey Kessler, who, "oversees export controls and does not have the personal relationship with Trump that Lutnick enjoys."

Earlier this week, the NYT reported Commerce paused its investigation into Megaspeed over whether it helped smuggle Nvidia's AI chips to China despite U.S. export controls.

Commerce, the NYT reported, passed the probe into Megaspeed off to the Department of Justice (DOJ), due to concerns around Kessler's handling of the probe. Neither agency confirmed this and the DOJ declined to comment.

While he led Nvidia, Huang faced criticism from lawmakers over his push to sell less advanced chips to China, despite tight export controls. His alliance with Trump helped him successfully lobby the administration to loosen controls and greenlight sales of advanced H200 chips to Beijing last year.

Now, some lawmakers are calling on Lutnick to answer for this shift.

Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Ore.), ranking member of the Senate Finance Committee, and Rep. Richard Neal (D-Mass.), the top Democrat on the House Ways and Means Committee, told Lutnick in a Thursday letter to preserve his department's records on Trump's H200 decision.

"There appears to be a profound lack of due diligence in Commerce's process for approving these Chinese buyers of Nvidia chips," the lawmakers wrote.

Regardless of Lutnick's future at the agency, tech analysts are anticipating new policy changes, from Congress and Commerce, as national security concerns remain high.

On Capitol Hill, Huang's departure is spurring momentum for chip export bills' inclusion in the annual defense spending bill.

And Commerce "is under pressure to do things," Beacon Policy Advisors managing partner Stephen Myrow told The Hill.

"On the other hand, they need to make sure whatever they do doesn't upset the applecart with China that it triggers a renewed export control fight where access to rare earth critical minerals gets supply chained," he said.

Trump and his Cabinet have walked a delicate line with China amid a tight race on AI development and an intermittent trade war .

The mounting scrutiny on the Trump administration comes as the president prepares to head to China next week for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit.

While there, Trump expects to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, he said last Sunday.

Ian Bremmer, the founder of GZERO Media, said stricter export controls from the federal government in response to the Nvidia-Megaspeed scandal would spark Chinese retaliation and put "pressure" on the relationship between Trump and Xi.

"This is a serious threat to what has been, over the past months, a reasonably warmly managed and very engaged relationship," Bremmer said in a video . "And it's not at all clear that can continue even through the remainder of the Trump administration."

He appeared on CNN’s “State of the Union,” Fox News’s “Fox News Sunday,” NBC News’s “Meet the Press,” and CBS News’s “Face the Nation” to discuss the cause of the ground stop, which is still not known, and the…
articles.body:
Treasury Secretary Sean Duffy on Sunday pinned Friday’s nationwide ground stop on Congress’s lack of funding.

He appeared on CNN’s “State of the Union,” Fox News’s “Fox News Sunday,” NBC News’s “Meet the Press,” and CBS News’s “Face the Nation” to discuss the cause of the ground stop, which is still not known, and the aftermath .

President Trump echoed the claim on Sunday. “If Congress approves the desperately needed money for Air Traffic Control, we can get it built quickly and efficiently. It will be the BEST SYSTEM anywhere in the World,” the president wrote in a Truth Social post .

It was only the third of such stoppage to happen in the U.S. since the Sept. 11, 2001, terror attacks. The secretary has asserted the need to ground flights resulted from a telecommunications contractor error as opposed to bad actors, using the incident to bolster his calls for increased air infrastructure funding in two subsequent press conferences.

Duffy’s fellow Trump administration cabinet member, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, is also slated to sit for a television interview Sunday. The top Democrats on the House’s and Senate’s respective trade committees asked his department last week to preserve its records on President Trump’s decision to green light Nvidia’s sale of powerful computer chips to China — a request that came after the tech company’s CEO resigned in light of reports he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

Meanwhile, Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) called it a “bunch of nonsense” that he can’t win Senate Majority Leader over Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) in response to a report from The Hill that alleged Senate insiders close to Schumer believed the Maryland Senator was using the leadership contest to win concessions on Medicare-for-All and terminating the filibuster.

During his appearance, Van Hollen said his support in the upper chamber was growing and revealed he already had the backing of 15 senators.

Trump himself has no public events scheduled for Sunday, as was true for Saturday. He is set to travel to China later this week, where he will engage in a high-stakes trilateral meeting with the presidents of Russia and China, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping, respectively.

articles.title: Trump breaks silence on nationwide ground stop and demands more money from Congress
articles.summary: WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump on Sunday broke his silence on the nationwide ground stop that snarled airline travel this weekend, using the incide...
articles.body:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump on Sunday broke his silence on the nationwide ground stop that snarled airline travel this weekend, using the incident to push Congress on money to fully upgrade America's air traffic control system.

The Republican president has been conspicuously quiet on the ground stop since it began Friday afternoon, instead issuing statements on social media about completely different topics as frustrated passengers were left stranded at airports and his government scrambled with airlines to restore normal travel.

Trump said in a new post on his social media platform that his administration has begun upgrading that system, but that the task should not be done in "drips and drabs." The Republican-controlled Congress approved $12.5 billion for the Federal Aviation Administration as part of the party's sweeping tax cut package last year, but Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy has repeatedly characterized that funding as an down payment on a broader overhaul of the aging system.

"If Congress approves the desperately needed money for Air Traffic Control, we can get it built quickly and efficiently," Trump wrote on social media Sunday. "It will be the BEST SYSTEM anywhere in the World. Much of our current air control system is 50 years old - RIDICULOUS!"

In another post, he complained about how his Democratic predecessor had maintained the FAA and the air traffic control system, accusing Joe Biden's administration of making an "old and broken system worse than when they began."

Biden signed a massive infrastructure bill into law in the first year of his presidency, which set aside $25 billion for the FAA to improve airports and its traffic control towers, to redevelop airport terminals, to "upgrade the foundation" of the air traffic control system, according to the FAA.

Duffy was the administration's public face on the ground stop across the Sunday news shows, pressing Congress for billions of dollars for upgrades to the air traffic control infrastructure.

"I can't apologize for what was passed on to us. And I can't blame Republicans or Democrats, because it's all of them. It goes back, 20, 25, 30 years of a lack of investment," he told NBC's "Meet the Press."

In a post on the social media platform X, Duffy said contractor L3Harris Technologies Inc. had secured two routers from FAA facilities in Texas and Arkansas and was conducting "deep diagnostics" on the equipment. He has said the problem began when L3Harris was replacing a section of old copper wire with new fiber wire, somehow causing the system to overload.

After the wire was replaced at the site in El Dorado, Ark., and the router was turned on, a problem then cropped up at a facility in Amarillo, Texas, cascading into the ground stop. "We didn't think that should or would happen, he told ABC's "This Week."

As for the traveling public, he told CBS' "Face the Nation" that "we have some delays in the airspace right now," but looking to the end of the day and into Monday, "we should be running at full capacity."

In a ground stop, airplanes and crews are taken out of position, he said, "so it takes a little bit of time for the airliners to get back … at full capacity and operation but we're well on our way."

articles.title: Suspected China spy linked to Nvidia's ex-boss left in 2025, Megaspeed says
articles.summary: The Nvidia scandal has raised questions over whether advanced AI chips ended up in China, despite US restrictions.
articles.body:
Alice Huang, a suspected China spy who has been linked to Nvidia's former boss Jensen Huang, left her executive role at Megaspeed in August last year, the company says.

Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive of the AI chip-making giant Nvidia after it emerged he had allegedly had affairs with Alice Huang as well as with one of his employees.

Megaspeed is the biggest buyer of Nvidia chips in south-east Asia and the scandal at Nvidia has raised questions about the possibility that high-end AI chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions.

The Singapore-based company said on Sunday it had launched an internal investigation into its business.

It said it was aware of reports "containing assertions about our business, supply chain and global operations that are not supported by verifiable evidence".

It added that it "conducts legitimate and lawful business" and has "retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation".

On Friday, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent blamed fellow Trump cabinet colleague Howard Lutnick's commerce department for failing to properly oversee the export of high-end chips.

Bessent told CNBC that several agencies "were in favour of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months... but Commerce has the pen... and you will have to ask them about their internal process".

The so-called entity list restricts US trade with overseas firms and individuals.

Lutnick has been called to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next month over his department's role in allowing Nvidia to export its advanced chips.

Other congressional committees have asked both Lutnick and his department to retain all records relating to Nvidia and Jensen Huang.

Megaspeed is suspected of giving backdoor access to Nvidia chips to Chinese companies via its data centres in Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand.

Nvidia has been banned from selling its advanced chips to China.

While Singapore does not prohibit the transfer of advanced AI chips to companies abroad, such moves can breach US export controls.

Singapore has said that while it does not enforce "unilateral export controls imposed by other countries" it expects all companies in its jurisdiction to respect such regulations.

Megaspeed said it "designs and maintains its global operational and supply-chain control frameworks to comply with all applicable laws and regulatory regimes". It said this includes "US export control requirements and local jurisdiction rules in every market where we operate".

China has denied that Alice Huang is a spy and warned the US not to use the scandal as a "pretext for imposing a technological blockade" on AI technology.
