articles.title: Transportation secretary says he doesn’t apologize for FAA’s nationwide ground stop
articles.summary: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy declined to apologize for the nationwide ground stop that stranded hundreds of thousands of travelers across the country
articles.body: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy on Sunday declined to apologize for the nationwide ground stop on Friday that stranded hundreds of thousands of travelers across the country following a router issue that derailed air traffic control communications. Instead, the secretary blamed his predecessors and previous presidential administrations that he said did not do enough to modernize the nation’s air traffic control system. “It happened on my watch, but we have to be clear: I am moving at an incredible speed that no one has done at the FAA or in decades, and I’m proud of the work we’re doing, the attention we’re bringing to this issue,” Duffy told NBC News’ “Meet the Press.” “But I can’t apologize for what was passed off to us, and I can’t blame Republicans or Democrats because it’s all of them.” The secretary also blamed “30 years of a lack of investment,” from the country’s previous leaders. “Why they didn’t do that I don’t know, but they gave me a system that needs to be fixed, and President [Donald] Trump and I are going to fix it,” he added. His remarks come less than two days after the Federal Aviation Administration issued a national ground stop that lasted several hours, leading to thousands of flight cancellations beginning on Friday and continuing through the weekend. FAA contractor L3Harris was working on replacing a copper line with a fiber line at a remote site when the work led a router to overwhelm the national FAA telecommunications network, Duffy said Saturday. Duffy also said Sunday on “Meet the Press” that he expects airports and airlines to resume normal operations by the end of the day or early Monday morning. “By the end of today, into tomorrow, I think we’ll be back to normal,” he said, adding that Friday’s ground stop led airplanes and flight crews to be “out of position.” “It takes some time for the airlines to rechoreograph all of their crews and aircraft. We’re going to start seeing things get better today, but I think back to normal tomorrow,” Duffy said. The secretary also demurred when asked whether he could guarantee that a similar travel disruption won’t happen in the future. “First we have to figure out what happened. Was this a faulty installation by L3Harris that was doing their work for us? Was it a fault of the router itself? We have to do that investigation and make sure we take precautions. We don’t want to shut down the airspace,” Duffy told “Meet the Press” moderator Kristen Welker. “We’re going to figure out what was the root cause and then move forward from there, fixing how we do business at the FAA,” he added. Duffy also reiterated a call he’s made all weekend for more funding from Congress to modernize the nationwide air traffic control system, which has long been outdated and faced problems. “The president, since he came to office, has been pushing for modernization of the airspace. Before I was even sworn in, he brought this up,” the secretary said, pointing to $12.5 billion that was allocated for air traffic control improvements in a GOP-backed spending bill last year. “The Congress was very specific in how I spend that money. I have a certain allotment for radar, a certain allotment for radios, a certain allotment for building new infrastructure for my centers for air traffic controllers. They didn’t give me money for telecom. They didn’t give me money for new software,” Duffy said. “I’m coming back to Congress and the American people to explain all the great work we’re doing right now,” he continued. “We’re going to spend that $12.5 billion by the end of 2028, but I need the rest of the money for software and a new telecom architecture that will be way more resilient. I need that money so I can start that build.” On Saturday, NBC News reported that on Thursday, just one day before the ground stop, Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russell Vought sent a letter to members of Congress asking lawmakers for $30.1 billion to upgrade the United States’ aging airports and air traffic control system. They wrote: “This investment is critical to complete the modernization of our national airspace — delivering a resilient telecommunications backbone for air traffic controllers, modern hardware and software, state-of-the-art control towers, and world-class airport infrastructure. These investments will address current challenges, including weather-related delays, while preparing the National Airspace System for emerging demands, such as safely integrating air traffic with the growing space industry.” On Sunday, Duffy urged Congress to “just do it.” “I’m doing all I can to keep people safe,” he said. “But I’m also telling you, if you don’t give us the resources, we can’t complete the job. And this is — of all the partisanship — this is the most bipartisan thing in all of Washington. Democrats, Republicans, the president, everyone agrees on this. Let’s just do it.”

articles.title: Congress' incoming wealthiest member vows to crack down on politicians getting rich in office
articles.summary: Joe Strada said he plans to crack down on congressional insider trading and politicians enriching themselves, drawing on his rise from bowling alley mechanic.
articles.body: EXCLUSIVE: Rep.-elect Joe Strada, R-Fla., poised to become the wealthiest member of Congress, told Fox News Digital that he plans to crack down on politicians who enrich themselves while serving in public office when he takes office in January. Strada, who went from working as a bowling alley mechanic to owning a nationwide HVAC company, is expected to become Congress' richest member, according to Forbes. The incoming Republican argued that public office should be about serving Americans rather than accumulating personal wealth. "We need to make sure that we hold politicians accountable," Strada told Fox News Digital. "Nobody, and I mean nobody, should get rich in public office. We're there to serve the American people." "If you want to get rich, stay in the private sector. I went into business to get rich, not Washington, D.C. I'm going to Washington, D.C., to serve the American people," he continued. The congressman-elect said combating congressional insider trading and political profiteering would be among his priorities as he prepares to leave the private sector for Capitol Hill. Strada pointed to his own rise from a blue-collar worker to a successful businessman as proof that the American Dream remains achievable, arguing that excessive government intervention has made it harder for others to follow a similar path. "I started with nothing. I was a handyman at a bowling alley. If I can do it, other everyday Americans can. Government needs to get out of their way and help them succeed," Strada said. "It's so important to give people opportunity to succeed and achieve their version of the American dream, and now it's time to open that up." "That's what I plan to do in Washington, D.C., give every American the opportunity they need to succeed, prosper, open a small business and start a career," he added. "I'm living proof of it," Strada said, referring to his own success. The incoming Republican also warned that the growing popularity of democratic socialism and proposals for expanding government programs could undermine American entrepreneurship, innovation and small-business growth. "I think it's important to show people the opportunity. The talking points of ‘free this, free that’ sounds great, but we do not want to suppress the American people. We instead want to show them that their goals and ambitions are achievable," Strada said. "It was achievable for me. I never went to college, the thought of college was not even in conversation with my parents. Going to college for me was unachievable," he added. Strada said his early work experience taught him the importance of discipline and perseverance, values he believes should be emphasized to younger generations. "I knew I had to work, and I worked hard," Strada said, adding that young Americans could benefit from a greater emphasis on work ethic. "I think if we can instill that in young people today, they'd be better off." The congressman-elect also identified housing affordability as a major obstacle preventing Americans from achieving financial independence, pledging to pursue federal deregulation, lower construction material costs and workforce development initiatives to make homeownership more accessible. "Housing cost is ridiculous. I have so many examples of ways we can still build a high-quality home for substantially less money, and more Americans could live out their dream of owning a home," Strada said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP As he prepares to take office in January, Strada said he hopes to secure a seat on the House Appropriations Committee, where he believes his business experience would allow him to "best serve the American people."

articles.title: Van Hollen says ‘bunch of nonsense’ that he can’t win Senate majority leader
articles.summary: Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) calls it a “bunch of nonsense” that he can’t win Senate Majority Leader over Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) in response to a report from The Hill that alleged Senate insiders close to Schumer believed the Maryland Senator was using the leadership contest to win concessions on Medicare-for-All and terminating the…
articles.body:
Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) calls it a “bunch of nonsense” that he can’t win Senate Majority Leader over Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) in response to a report from The Hill that alleged Senate insiders close to Schumer believed the Maryland Senator was using the leadership contest to win concessions on Medicare-for-All and terminating the filibuster.

“That’s a bunch of nonsense. The reality is this is a very open race,” Van Hollen said during an appearance on “Fox News Sunday.”

“The reality is I agree with the American people and all our candidates who ran across the country that this is not about left versus right,” the Maryland senator continued.

Van Hollen said the race for Senate Majority Leader was about the “economic populous message we heard across the country” rather than “progressives or moderates or conservatives.”

“So, yes, we’re gonna hear a lot of people trying to scare members. Reality is my position has been lockstep with the positions that our candidates took and they’re reflecting the will of the American people,” he concluded.

His remarks come after The Hill reported Saturday that Schumer’s allies predicted he will get more than 40 votes in his leadership contest against Van Hollen.

During his appearance, Van Hollen said his support in the upper chamber was growing and revealed he already had the backing of 15 senators.

There has been lots of speculation around Schumer and Van Hollen’s lists as multiple progressive Senators have publicly pledged their support for the Maryland senator, while other establishment and centrist lawmakers have declined to share their opinions.

A Senate insider close to Schumer previously told The Hill that they believed the race for leadership was “distracting” and “counterproductive,” adding that Van Hollen wasn’t actively calling colleagues to lock down votes for a potential race until very recently.

Van Hollen made waves in the upper chamber for his progressive stances, including openly criticizing Israeli settler violence in Gaza and advocating for the return of Kilmar Abrego Garcia — a Maryland resident mistakenly deported but returned to the U.S.

He announced his candidacy for Senate leadership on Thursday, describing himself as an “underdog.” Van Hollen credited his decision to run because he didn’t think “you can close the trust deficit by simply returning to the status quo or business as usual.”

articles.title: Sen.-elect Scott Colom says investing in the South can help Democrats win ‘a durable majority’
articles.summary: Sen.-elect Scott Colom, D-Miss., emphasized in that Democrats need to invest more in southern states like Mississippi, where he flipped the seat blue for the first time in decades.
articles.body: Sen.-elect Scott Colom, D-Miss., emphasized on NBC News’ “Meet the Press” that Democrats need to invest more in Southern states like Mississippi, where he flipped a seat blue for the first time in decades. “What we need to do now as a Democratic Party is understand we can’t continue to allow that lack of investment to occur,” he said Sunday. Colom’s projected win this month brought Democrats to a 55-seat majority in the Senate, with Alaska’s Senate race yet to be called. His victory over Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, a Republican, marked a seismic political shift in a state that last elected a Democrat to the Senate 44 years ago and has not had a Black senator since the Reconstruction period. Colom has been vocal in calling for Democrats to focus more on states like Mississippi, a view he emphasized again on Sunday. “We need to put senators like myself in positions where we can deliver for the rural South, where we can be leaders in ways that show the voters in rural America that we care about them, the voters in the Deep South that we want them to be successful,” Colom said. “And if we do that, I think we can have a competitive elections every cycle and put ourselves in positions where we can have a durable majority,” he continued. In the same interview, Colom identified reshaping tariff policies as his top priority to reduce prices. “We’ve got to fight for low tariffs to lower costs that helps our farmers, because they lost customers as a result of these tariffs, and we need to do everything in our power to help them get those customers back,” Colom said. He also called for raising the minimum wage. The federal minimum wage sits at $7.25 per hour, and it has not been raised since 2009. NBC News exit polls indicated that the cost of living was a top priority for voters. NBC’s exit polls showed that 89% of voters considered the cost of living “crucial” or a “major factor” in thinking about their vote for Congress. The same exit polls found that 66% of voters believed Trump’s tariff policies hurt the national economy. Colom was also asked on “Meet the Press” about whether he would vote to restore nationwide rights to abortion. The Mississippi senator-elect has said he is “personally pro-life because I’m a Christian” and that he does not “believe in late-term abortions.” He also said he does not believe that victims of rape or incest should be “forced” to “have that child.” “I’ll study what’s right for my values and for Mississippi and try to represent those values in D.C. to the best of my abilities,” he said. One of the tasks remaining for Congress this year is for Democrats to select their party leadership. Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., announced last week that he would challenge Sen. Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., for the Senate majority leader position. Asked whom he planned to support, Colom said he was “in listening mode” and did not commit to either candidate. “I don’t know either one of them that well, so I’m going to listen to what other people tell me about them, and I’m going to figure out what are the things that people are doing well in leadership, what are the things they’re not doing well, and find out how we can work together to achieve results,” Colom said.

articles.title: NYC DSA urges AOC to run for president while planning to take over City Council
articles.summary: NYC's Democratic Socialists of America voted to urge AOC to run for president in 2028, but some resolutions sparked an AI-generated controversy.
articles.body: The New York City chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America overwhelmingly voted to urge Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., to run for president in 2028 on Saturday. NYC-DSA approved a resolution making the call in a 291 to 123 vote at the chapter's annual convention. Gustavo Gordillo, co-chair of the local DSA chapter, said the vote was not a formal endorsement, but is instead a "a commitment to encouraging and building the foundation for a presidential campaign." "AOC and New York City DSA are committed to building a stronger democratic socialist movement and DSA will create the conditions for a presidential campaign capable of advancing a working-class political agenda," Gordillo said at a press conference on Saturday. DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS OF AMERICA LEADER SAYS ‘MANY’ IN GROUP WOULD BE 'THRILLED' AT AOC IN 2028 The chapter also laid out its plans to take over New York City's City Council, among other resolutions. Several of the party's resolutions ran into controversy for appearing to be AI-generated, according to a report from Politico. When run through the AI detection tool Pangram, the 2029 City Council election resolution was rated 100% AI-generated, the outlet reported. Two other DSA resolutions were reportedly flagged as AI-generated as well, related to expanding DSA membership in community boards and interaction with South Asian communities. The chapter has a policy against AI usage and voted on Saturday to formally oppose the expansion of AI. NYC-DSA co-chair Grace Mausser pushed back on the accuracy of the Pangram results in a statement to Politico. AOC CAMPAIGN MEMO FRAMES GROWTH FROM PROGRESSIVE FIREBRAND TO NATIONAL DEMOCRATIC PARTY FORCE "We are highly skeptical of the results coming out of Pangram as resolutions are often authored and edited in consensus by multiple members," she said, adding that Pangram’s tools "are made by the same industry that’s scraped writers’ work without permission and now sells software to accuse people of not writing their own words," Mausser said. articles.title: Duffy pins ground stop on Congress’s lack of funding
articles.summary: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed his predecessors and Congress for failing to adequately fund the nation’s aging air traffic control system following a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. flights on Friday that disrupted air travel across the country. In an interview with CNN’s “State of the Union” on Sunday, Duffy renewed his call for…
articles.body:
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed his predecessors and Congress for failing to adequately fund the nation’s aging air traffic control system following a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. flights on Friday that disrupted air travel across the country.

In an interview with CNN’s “State of the Union” on Sunday, Duffy renewed his call for Congress to approve an additional $50 billion to modernize the system, arguing that decades of underinvestment have left critical aviation infrastructure outdated.

“$12.5 billion after decades of lack of investment is not nearly enough money to fix all the problems we have in the airspace,” Duffy said, referring to funding Congress previously approved for air traffic control upgrades.

Duffy argued that the funding was designated for specific improvements, including radios, radar and telecommunications equipment, and could not be used to address other deficiencies in the nation’s aviation infrastructure.

He pointed to deteriorating air traffic control towers, saying some facilities lack functioning elevators and air conditioning, while others have leaking roofs.

The transportation secretary also deflected when asked whether he bore responsibility for Friday’s disruption, telling CNN, “I take responsibility for what was given to me by prior administrations.”

“When we do work and things go wrong, of course I’m the secretary. But I also have to acknowledge what was delivered to me,” Duffy said. ”I have systems that are from the 90s. I have radar that are from the 60s and 70s.”

Democrats have questioned why the Trump administration was requesting tens of billions of dollars in additional funding when it had spent only a fraction of the money already allocated by Congress.

In an interview with CNN, Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) pushed back on Duffy for deflecting the blame onto Congress, saying that it has met the requests.

“It’s really rich to hear the secretary pointing the fingers at Congress when Congress has given the administration what they asked for,” Van Hollen said Sunday. “If they need more, they should come up and justify it. I will support what is necessary to have a safe system and a reliable system.”

articles.title: Buttigieg takes swipe at Trump administration amid FAA flight chaos
articles.summary: Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg joked he'd help travelers rebook flights at a hotel bar after the FAA's nationwide ground stop Friday.
articles.body: DENVER — Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg took a swipe at the Trump administration’s handling of Friday’s nationwide FAA ground stop, joking that he would help stranded travelers rebook flights as delays and cancellations continued. I’ll begin with a public service announcement," Buttigieg told reporters in Denver. "I will be available in the hotel bar following the concert for anybody who needs to rebook their flights or get a refund per your rights." He made the remark as the "What’s Next" conference wrapped up in Denver. The two-day gathering, hosted by Majority Democrats, brought leaders together to discuss the party’s direction after its midterm victories. DEMS DESCEND ON DENVER TO SIZE UP 2028; WE ASKED WHO WANTS IN THE RACE The FAA lifted the ground stop shortly after 8 p.m. Friday, more than four hours after it began, but flights remained delayed and canceled over the weekend. The agency cited safety concerns and serious air traffic control communications issues. Buttigieg, who said he had no inside information about the cause of the ground stop, later questioned why the aviation system’s safeguards had not prevented an outage of that scale. He said he was watching the disruption as a traveler with a flight scheduled for Saturday. "The system has many redundancies in it, so that normally, if there’s one point of failure, something else can catch it," he said. "It is not clear to me why that redundancy did not prevent an outage of this magnitude." SCHUMER'S LEADERSHIP RIVAL REVEALS MAJOR SENATE RULE CHANGE HE'D PURSUE IF ELECTED Meanwhile, Trump administration officials offered a mixed account of the failure. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the cause remained under investigation, including whether a contractor made an error or equipment failed. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin later said the stoppage was not caused by artificial intelligence or a cyberattack, but by aging infrastructure that needs to be updated. President Donald Trump told Fox News that the system had broken down because of its age. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Friday’s disruption was the second nationwide ground stop since the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks. The first came in January 2023, when the FAA paused domestic departures for about 90 minutes because of an outage in its Notice to Air Missions system, which provides pilots with safety information. The FAA said at the time it found no evidence of a cyberattack. Buttigieg ordered a review of that outage and directed the agency to report on what happened and recommend steps to prevent a recurrence.

articles.title: Pence calls Vance ‘wrong’ on Iran war, GOP midterm losses
articles.summary: Former Vice President Mike Pence said Vice President Vance was “wrong” about attributing the Iran war to the GOP’s midterm losses, where the party lost control of Congress. Appearing on NBC’s “Meet the Press,” Pence stated Vance was a “good man” but disagreed with the statement, saying it was “wrong.” “We didn’t lose this midterm…
articles.body:
Former Vice President Mike Pence said Vice President Vance was “wrong” about attributing the Iran war to the GOP’s midterm losses, where the party lost control of Congress .

Appearing on NBC’s “Meet the Press,” Pence stated Vance was a “good man” but disagreed with the statement, saying it was “wrong.”

“We didn’t lose this midterm election because of the war. I think part of the reason why voters were turned off was because after seeing our military respond brilliantly in Operation Epic Fury and the strike against Iran last year, for inexplicable reasons, we stopped after five weeks,” he continued.

In his statement, Vance wrote that “many people who voted for Trump/Vance in 2024 voted for Democrats in 2026” due to anger over the Iran war, cost of living and inflation, not focusing on putting America first and the current U.S. relationship with Israel.

Pence lauded the military victories in Iran — including taking down thousands of military sites — though he recalled an old saying: “You don’t make peace with your enemy, you make peace with your defeated enemy.”

“You need look no further than Bahrain in the last 24 hours where Iran is still firing on U.S. targets, to see the Iranians don’t give evidence of feeling defeated,” the former vice president said, adding that he believed Americans were frustrated that the U.S. military “stopped short.”

The Council on Foreign Relations released an analysis last week that calculated the Democratic party picked up 44 seats in the House and is enjoying its largest margin over Republicans since the 1990 midterms. In the Senate, Democrats flipped 8 seats, with the Alaska race yet to be called, tied for third for the biggest net seat gain for any midterm election since 1942.

“I have to believe that that was a reflection in some respects of some of the voices of isolationism on the right that have gained some perches for this administration,” Pence concluded.

The conflict with Iran has lasted over eight months, with President Trump telling reporters at a surprise White House briefing that the conflict was “effectively over” but later stating on Veterans Day that the “question is when we want to end. We must have a total victory.”

The war’s costs have ballooned since its start on Feb. 28, totaling an estimated $47.1 billion in October.

articles.title: Van Hollen: Senators who pledged to support Schumer will switch vote
articles.summary: Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) said that several senators whom Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer’s (D-N.Y.) team claimed would vote for him have privately pledged to back Van Hollen instead for majority leader. The Hill reported on Saturday that Schumer’s allies expect him to win more than 40 votes in the race for Senate majority…
articles.body:
Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) said that several senators whom Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer’s (D-N.Y.) team claimed would vote for him have privately pledged to back Van Hollen instead for majority leader.

The Hill reported on Saturday that Schumer’s allies expect him to win more than 40 votes in the race for Senate majority leader and believe the Maryland Democrat is using his challenge to push for concessions on progressive priorities, including “Medicare for All” and eliminating the filibuster.

“Schumer’s team put out a list just the other day of people they said who are voting for Senator Schumer,” Van Hollen said on CNN’s “State of the Union” on Sunday. “I can tell you that a number of those people on that list have actually committed to voting for me, and the others are very open to the idea of change.”

Van Hollen, who is challenging Schumer to lead Senate Democrats when the party takes control of the chamber in January, did not identify which senators had privately pledged their support or specify how many votes he had secured.

He insisted that he had a path to victory, arguing that Democratic senators are increasingly open to replacing their longtime leader and earn the trust of voters.

“There’s a hunger for change within the Senate Democratic Caucus,” Van Hollen said.

But he insisted he had a path to victory, arguing that Democratic senators are increasingly open to replacing their longtime leader.

“There is a hunger for change within the Senate Democratic Caucus,” Van Hollen said.

He framed his challenge as a response to voters’ demands for change following the midterm elections, arguing that Democrats should not return to business as usual.

“This really is a response to the call of voters, who clearly rejected [President] Donald Trump and his awful policies. But they haven’t fully hired Democrats,” he said.

He outlined several differences with Schumer, including his belief that Democratic leaders should stay out of contested party primaries.

Van Hollen accused Schumer of working with AIPAC and cryptocurrency interests to defeat two candidates who ultimately won their races.

As of Sunday, Van Hollen has secured public endorsements from Sens. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.), along with Sens.-elect Abdul El-Sayed (D-Mich.) and Peggy Flanagan (D-Minn.).

Schumer, meanwhile, has received public backing from more than a dozen senators, including incoming Democratic Whip Brian Schatz (Hawaii) and Sens. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.), Tammy Baldwin (D-Wis.), Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.) and Kirsten Gillibrand (D-N.Y.).

articles.title: This week on The Hill: House and Senate race to wrap up business before recess
articles.summary: Both chambers are back in Washington this week for a final push to move legislation and wrap up business before leaving for the one-week Thanksgiving recess. House Democrats are set to hold their leadership elections on Wednesday and Thursday, as the party prepares to take control of the chamber next year. House Republicans held their…
articles.body:
Both chambers are back in Washington this week for a final push to move legislation and wrap up business before leaving for the one-week Thanksgiving recess.

House Democrats are set to hold their leadership elections on Wednesday and Thursday, as the party prepares to take control of the chamber next year.

House Republicans held their leadership elections last week, where House Judiciary Committee Chair Jim Jordan (R-Ohio) was chosen to be the minority leader. House GOP Whip Tom Emmer (R-Minn.) and House GOP Conference Chair Lisa McClain (R-Mich.) won their reelection bids.

In the Senate, lawmakers are expected to hold a procedural vote on an amendment to the permitting reform bill, setting up the possibility of a final vote on the legislation later this week. The bill would speed up the build-out of the nation’s infrastructure, especially energy projects.

The Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions (HELP) Committee, meanwhile, is scheduled to vote on two executive branch nominations: Heidi Overton, to serve as commissioner of the Food and Drug Administration (FDA), and James O’Neill for director of the National Science Foundation (NSF).

Overton is a prominent supporter of Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s “Make America Healthy Again” movement. She stood alongside President Trump in August when he announced an executive order aimed at scaling back childhood vaccine schedules.

Democrats to hold leadership elections: Democrats will choose who they want to lead their conference next year on Wednesday and Thursday.

Senate HELP Committee to vote on Overton, O’Neill: Both Overton and O’Neill are on a rocky path, as one Republican defector on the panel could sink their nominations.

Senate continues work on permitting reform bill: The upper chamber will hold a procedural vote on a substitute amendment to the bill on Monday.

Democratic leadership elections to take place

House Democrats will select their next leadership team in a closed-door process this week, with members casting secret ballots to determine who will lead the conference.

In the top tiers, there are no contested races and, therefore, no anticipated shake-ups.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) is expected to be nominated for a history-making promotion to become the first Black Speaker in U.S. history.

Reps. Katherine Clark (D-Mass.) and Pete Aguilar (D-Calif.) are seeking to become majority leader and majority whip, respectively.

Rep. Ted Lieu (D-Calif.) is seeking to replace Aguilar as the party’s caucus chair, while Rep. Joe Neguse (D-Colo.) is running for assistant speaker, a position unique to the Democratic Caucus.

The only contested leadership race is to replace Lieu as caucus vice chair. Two Democrats, Reps. Sara Jacobs (D-Calif.) and Lauren Underwood (D-Ill.), are competing for the post.

Jacobs wrote in a Dear Colleague letter back in August that she believes the role of the vice chair is “fundamentally Member-focused: helping every Member feel heard, supported, and connected to something larger than their own office or district.”

“In particular, I want to help bring our Caucus together before the hardest moments arrive, and help us navigate them when they do…As your Vice Chair, I would use my expertise and experience to ensure those family conversations happen and are as productive as possible,” Jacobs wrote in the letter, obtained by Punchbowl News.

Underwood, meanwhile, wrote in her letter circulated to colleagues this month that House Democrats “have an urgent mandate from our constituents, and we need the talents of every single Member to take on the Trump Administration’s chaos and corruption.”

“We need everyone’s input, everyone’s ideas, and everyone’s bills, and we won’t let sharp elbows stop us from solving problems,” Underwood said in her letter, obtained by Punchbowl News. “As Vice Chair, I’ll prioritize keeping our Caucus convenings a place of trust, where every Member is respected, we proactively take on the tough issues, and our shared goals are not undermined by leaks or turf wars.”

All of those positions will be solidified by week’s end — with the exception of the Speakership. For Jeffries, the caucus vote is only the first step. The full House will formally elect its Speaker in a floor vote on Jan. 3, when the 120th Congress convenes.

Jeffries needs 218 votes to win the gavel. And despite a handful of incoming Democrats who have declined to commit to supporting Jeffries, the Democrats’ large majority next year gives him plenty of cushion to absorb defections. Heading in, Jeffries is nothing if not confident in the outcome.

“You think I don’t have the votes nailed down?” he asked a reporter last week.

Senate HELP Committee to hold vote on key nominations

The committee will meet on Wednesday to vote on Overton, whom Trump tapped back in August to lead the FDA, and O’Neill, whom Trump nominated to serve as the director of the NSF.

Republicans have just a single vote majority on the panel, so losing one member would be enough to sink the nomination if all Democrats oppose it.

Committee Chair Bill Cassidy (R-La.) said he met with Overton on Tuesday but remained undecided on her nomination, as well as O’Neill’s. In a post on X, Cassidy seemingly tied the nominations to promises Kennedy made to secure Cassidy’s support for his confirmation, which have since been broken.

“While I remain undecided on both of their nominations and am aware that other Republican members of the Committee are undecided as well, the Committee is moving forward with noticing their markup in the hopes of resolving their path forward one way or another this Congress,” Cassidy wrote.

Cassidy, a physician, previously criticized Overton’s involvement in the Trump administration’s efforts to roll back childhood vaccination, calling it “almost disqualifying.” He indicated Overton would need to repudiate Trump’s comments to secure his vote.

Overton, a physician, is a top White House domestic policy adviser on health issues. If confirmed, she would take over an agency roiled by an exodus of top staff and viewed by many in the healthcare industry as less trustworthy and more politicized than it has been in any previous administration.

Sen. Patty Murray (D-Wash.), a senior member of the HELP committee, had grilled Overton on her abortion stance back in a September hearing.

“Well, despite what FDA says, and what decades of science says, you actually published an article three years ago that incorrectly described medication abortion as ‘dangerous to women.’ The fact that you would blatantly contradict decades of high-quality scientific evidence, and millions of patients use it, is alarming to me,” Murray said then.

Senate to hold procedural vote on permitting reform bill amendment

The upper chamber will hold a procedural vote Monday on a substitute amendment, sponsored by Sen. Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.Va.), that would make some technical changes to a bipartisan permitting reform bill.

A final vote on the bill could come as early as this week, but it isn’t guaranteed.

The permitting reform bill, dubbed the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, would make changes to the nation’s environmental laws that could make it easier to build projects and make it harder to block them, with either lawsuits or other legal mechanisms.

Trump has gone after renewable energy projects, and the bill contains measures that would protect those that are already approved — a sweetener for Democrats.

The bill is a compromise between Democrats, who want to build out more renewable energy, and Republicans, who want to build more fossil fuel energy and generally support curtailing environmental regulations in the name of economic growth.

The White House is also backing the bill, even as Trump insisted Monday that he would not approve any wind projects and that the legislation was still subject to negotiations. Its fate in the House, however, is unclear as some Democrats and Republicans in the lower chamber have called for changes to the bill.

Rachel Frazin and Nathaniel Weixel contributed to this report.

articles.title: Republicans must embrace early voting to win again
articles.summary: Early voting has a serious economy of scale advantage, allowing a political party’s turnout operations to get more bang for their buck.
articles.body:
Democrats sailed to a crushing victory in the midterm elections, partly on the strength of their under-discussed decisive advantage in early voting.

Democrats so far flipped eight Republican Senate seats in states including Texas, Kansas, South Carolina, Iowa, Ohio and Mississippi, and could potentially flip Alaska. In the House, Democrats flipped over 40 seats with a 13 point generic ballot advantage. In contrast, Republicans flipped one congressional seat in Maine . Governors’ results were similarly devastating to the Republicans.

An underdiscussed factor in the Republican’s recent electoral underperformance was conservatives’ refusal to vote early at the same rate as liberals. Registered Democrats accounted for roughly 45 percent of early ballots versus 30 percent for Republicans, almost identical to their margin of victory.

A good example of this outcome comes from Texas’ governor race. Third term Republican Gov. Greg Abbot received roughly the same number of votes in 2026 than in 2022 . He was defeated by Democrat Gina Hinojosa, who received almost 1.7 million more votes in 2026 than 2022 Democratic nominee Beto O’Rourke.

A 2026 Abbot would have easily beaten much hyped 2022 O’Rourke, but Democrats benefited from surging turnout relative to the previous midterm. Hinojosa actually got more Texas votes during a midterm than Kamala Harris did in a presidential election . This turnout surge contributed more to the Democrats’ victories than swing votes.

If Republicans want to remain a viable political party, they simply must embrace early voting as a core turnout tool. It is no longer optional to prevent the Democrats’ next perfect storm.

The first rule of voter mobilization is to make it as easy as possible for your people to vote while spending as little as possible. Democrats play to win, while Republicans aren’t even really on the field. Democrats operate whole enterprises driving their voters to the polls during early voting, while most Republican turnout operations are effectively outsourced.

Early voting has a serious economy of scale advantage, allowing a political party’s turnout operations to get more bang for their buck.

It is simply more expensive per voter to hire 10 vans for a single day for 10 trips moving 100 people to the polls, rather than hiring just one van for the entire early voting period and using it 100 times over the course of that much greater length of time. This is vastly more efficient per dollar than relying on a single day surge.

If fully embraced, early voting could actually be more of an advantage for Republicans, because Republican-led states have higher rates of employment and Republicans are more likely to be active in a religious community , be married and have children . Liberals are more likely to be single, childless and states led by liberals have more people living in their parents’ basements and posting on social media as a kind of substitute.

Living a busy, productive life is a good thing and related to conservatives’ being happier, more satisfied, and having better mental health than liberals. But it also means that conservatives have less time to obsess over politics, and less time to vote out of competing life priorities.

On a personal note, I would have missed Virginia’s 2025 election due to a family flu if I hadn’t banked my vote early. The flexibility of early voting makes casting a ballot easier for people living full lives with changing family schedules, the kind of people who mostly vote Republican. I have also been personally told by many voters that they’ll vote on election day “as God intended,” so I’m well aware of the difficulty in altering this preference.

This isn’t the first time Republicans lost a winnable race due to failures adopting early voting. Nevada Democratic Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto narrowly won reelection in 2022 over Republican nominee Adam Laxalt likely due to a serious snowstorm . Laxalt even tweeted a “weather alert.”

This matters. One study found that for every inch of rainfall, turnout decreases by nearly 1 percent, and for every inch of snowfall it decreases by half a percent. Given how Republicans currently win a much larger percentage of the Election Day vote , it isn’t an exaggeration to say that storm cost Republicans a Senate seat. As long as Republicans rely heavily on Election Day turnout, their fate is literally at the mercy of the weather.

In 2024, Trump and the Republican National Committee more actively encouraged early voting , so our early vote numbers rose and narrowed Democrat’s early edge, resulting in electoral victory. Nothing on a similar scale was attempted in 2026.

When confronted with these facts, Republicans often express a desire to simply end early voting and return to Election Day instead of election month. If Republicans want to change that, they first need to win elections. Doing that without early voting is like bringing a knife to a gunfight.

Republican leaders need to adjust to that reality and signal that it’s wise for Republican voters to vote early. It will take many years and electoral cycles to dig out of the hole Republicans are now in. Best to get started today.

Andrew Follett conducts research analysis for a Washington nonprofit. area.

articles.title: Huckabee Sanders doesn’t rule out future presidential bid
articles.summary: Arkansas Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders (R) on Sunday left open the possibility of a future presidential run, saying she is focused on leading her state but stopped short of ruling out a bid for the White House. In an interview with CNN’s “State of the Union” on Sunday, Sanders was asked about her political future…
articles.body:
Arkansas Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders (R) on Sunday left open the possibility of a future presidential run, saying she is focused on leading her state but stopped short of ruling out a bid for the White House.

In an interview with CNN’s “State of the Union” on Sunday, Sanders was asked about her political future and whether her father, former Arkansas Gov. Mike Huckabee (R), would support her following in his footsteps by running for president.

“I don’t know,” Sanders, who won reelection for her second and final term as governor, said with a laugh. “Given the fact that he knows what that means, I’m not sure he would wish that on me in some cases.”

Her father unsuccessfully sought the Republican presidential nomination in 2008 and 2016, winning the Iowa caucuses during his first campaign. Sanders helped run her father’s campaign operation in 2008.

When CNN host Dana Bash pressed Sanders about her own presidential ambitions, the governor emphasized that she was happy in her current role but did not completely rule out a presidential run.

“For me, personally, I just got reelected as the governor of Arkansas. I love what I’m doing, and I look forward to holding this job for the next four years,” Sanders said. “My plan is to focus and do as best as I can lifting up the people of my state, moving my state forward, and really just keep my focus there for right now.”

Bash asked if Sanders was committing to serving her full four-year term as governor, which would extend beyond the 2028 presidential election.

“Well, at that point I’m termed out anyway unless they change the rules,” Sanders joked. “My max out is in four years, they’re going to kick me out whether I like it or not. But ultimately the simple answer is I like what I’m doing.”

Sanders served as White House press secretary during President Trump’s first term before becoming the first woman elected governor of Arkansas in 2022. Much like other possible contenders with presidential ambitions, Sanders recently released a memoir titled “Unapologetic: Clarity and Conviction in a World Gone Crazy.”

articles.title: For Democrats, it is time to get serious
articles.summary: Democratic lawmakers failed to attend a pivotal House vote on the potential impeachment of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, allowing Republicans to bury the measure despite allegations of misconduct during unauthorized military operations.
articles.body:
Democrats have spent months arguing that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is unfit for his position and should be removed from office. As someone who spent 15 years working for eight secretaries of Defense, I believe they were right.

Hegseth’s defenders might argue that Hegseth’s norm-shattering behavior may be merely aberrant or illegal, and that the executive branch’s leeway to conduct extended military operations without congressional approval has long been contested. However, there is little doubt that Hegseth has overseen extrajudicial killings , human rights abuses, and violations of the law of armed conflict in Venezuela and Iran. If those actions don’t constitute “high crimes and misdemeanors,” those words no longer have a coherent meaning.

When Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) forced a vote on whether to impeach Hegseth, Democrats had one job: show up to vote. Instead, 11 Democrats did not turn up for the vote , which allowed the Republicans — by a seven vote margin — to bury the measure in committee for the rest of this Congress.

The missing Democrats offered a flurry of excuses for their absences, but their explanations were unserious and unacceptable. Most of them got stuck in traffic on the way to Capitol Hill from a party celebrating their recent midterm victories. Even Speaker Emerita Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.) missed the vote — she was in California receiving an award .

These explanations wouldn’t fly if they were coming from a first-term city councilor missing a routine vote, let alone members of the world’s most important legislative body considering the impeachment of a Cabinet secretary waging an unauthorized war costing the lives of American service members and nearly $50 billion in taxpayer dollars to date.

The Democrats’ failure in this instance has arguably strengthened Hegseth and handed President Trump the opportunity to proclaim, however ludicrously, that the vote was an “ EXONERATION ” for his embattled Defense secretary.

Some Democrats have suggested the public shouldn’t be concerned about this episode, as they will simply impeach Hegseth at the start of the new Congress in 2027, when Democrats will control both chambers. This is cold comfort. With Massie departing Congress, a renewed effort to impeach Hegseth will be viewed as a purely partisan exercise. Moreover, if conviction and removal from office is the Democrats’ true objective, the Senate arithmetic may also be less favorable next year.

Yes, there will be more Democrats in place, but the body won’t include lame ducks like Sens. John Cornyn (R-Texas), Joni Ernst (R-Iowa), Thom Tillis (R-N.C.), or Susan Collins (R-Maine), who, with nothing left to lose politically, may have been willing to defy the president in a parting act of courage. This possibility has now been squandered.

This episode also raises uncomfortable questions about the readiness of Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) and his leadership team to assume the governing responsibilities with which the voters have entrusted them. If Jeffries and his whip operation cannot ensure every available member is present for such a consequential vote, it begs the question of whether he has the toughness and discipline to be a worthy successor to Speaker Pelosi, who long ran the caucus with exacting control.

Zooming out from this individual episode, Democrats must remember that, after the discord of the Vietnam era, it took a generation of Democrats to persuade voters that the party could be trusted with national security once again. Senators like Sam Nunn (D-Ga.), Carl Levin (D-Mich), and yes, Joe Biden (D-Del.), along with leaders like Secretary of State Madeleine Albright and Defense Secretary William Perry, rebuilt public confidence through their steady comportment and command of the issues.

That credibility was hard-won, and it can be lost far quicker than it was earned. Democrats cannot appear cavalier about a matter as grave as impeaching the secretary of Defense and expect voters to regard them as responsible stewards of America’s interests.

Democrats were able to win the recent midterms almost by default; they should recognize that voters turned out not so much to support them as cast their ballots against Trump’s follies on the Iran war, tariffs, the cost of living, and so much else. The Democrats are yet to put forward a coherent vision of their own, including on international affairs and national security, and the upcoming fights over the National Defense Authorization Act and funding restrictions on the Iran war — for which the administration wants another $70 billion — will be a key test of how Democrats handle themselves.

Republicans, for their part, are putting their most hard-nosed figures out front over the next two years, including new White House chief of staff Stephen Miller and incoming Minority Leader Jim Jordan (R-Ohio). One need not admire their politics, or even view them as competent, to recognize that these individuals have never been reluctant to show up for a fight. Democrats must match that level of focus and commitment if they are to carry out the mandate they won this November.

As President Obama urged in his 2009 inaugural address, Democrats must “set aside childish things,” like half-hearted excuses for missing pivotal votes, and start getting serious about doing their jobs. If not, their governing majorities may be short-lived and their chances of taking back the White House in 2029 will be imperiled.

Greg Pollock served in a series of leadership positions in the Office of the U.S. Secretary of Defense from 2010-2025, including twice serving as an acting deputy assistant secretary of Defense. He is now an adjunct professor at Georgetown University’s School of Foreign Service and a non-resident senior fellow at the Center for Climate and Security.

articles.title: Could Trump turn against the AI barons?
articles.summary: Following recent election losses, Donald Trump signaled potential shifts in AI policy, including increased regulation of tech leaders and cooperation with Democrats on safety measures.
articles.body:
Pulverized by the blue wave, President Trump hinted at several policy volte-faces when he spoke with Ross Douthat on “60 Minutes” last Sunday. He’d work with Democrats on AI safety, for one. Summoning his inner Bernie Sanders, he turned tough guy on the AI barons. “We had a situation where somebody was reported to us to be doing something bad with AI,” Trump remarked . “We called them very strongly and said, ‘Get ready to go to jail. Please give your wife a kiss good night.’”

So much for “ self-policing ,” the formula he had been offering mere weeks earlier. It’s possible that the unnamed AI baron was Jensen Huang (The New York Times reported Trump was briefed on the matter a year before the story broke ), though there’s no evidence to establish the connection. Days after the recording of Trump’s interview came the revelations over the Nvidia CEO’s alleged indiscretions: Huang apologized for cheating on his wife amid reports of a fling with Alice Huang, a former executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based Nvidia customer, whom U.S. intelligence reportedly believes to be a Chinese spy. Trump, no stranger to the sex scandal, is sympathetic. He called Huang an “honorable guy.”

The political fallout might yet give him something concrete to latch onto as he reassesses AI policy. What better way to persuade the president than a vivid example? This may be the turn in the weather for which the right’s advocates of AI regulation have been praying.

In the run-up to Election Day, I chatted with Steve Bannon, who relished the prospect of prying Trump loose from the tech donor class. “Much of the campaign cash that came in at scale late was from the oligarchs,” he said. “They will demand their pound of flesh. That is when the real fight begins.” The oligarchs, he added, are “rightly enormously unpopular.”

Last week’s shellacking of Republicans gave Bannon and his allies much to work with — AI being one of several key issues Democrats used to appeal to voters. In Texas, Democrat Gina Hinojosa hammered Republican Gov. Greg Abbott (R) for promoting the state as the “ epicenter of AI development .” His belated turn against data centers couldn’t save him. In South Carolina, Democrat Annie Andrews upset Sen. Darline Graham (R) after branding her “Data Center Darline.”

Elements of both the right and the left are now, at full throttle, moving toward data center moratoria and public ownership stakes in AI. Agreement on those measures, though, leaves considerable room for disagreement about their purpose. Bannon described bans on Chinese nationals working at frontier AI labs and receiving student visas as “the next data center and Flock camera fight.” His vision of technological competition with China sits uneasily alongside the argument of Democrats like Texas Rep. Greg Casar, that “the AI arms race is not a race that you win.”

Of the arguments available for bringing the companies to heel, the populist right’s America First pitch seems best suited to Trump’s instincts. It casts the AI labs as reckless custodians of the national interest. James Fishback, the failed longshot populist Republican candidate for Florida governor earlier this year, captured its blend of economic anxiety and nationalism when he told me in July that “we’re interested in middle class fears [now that] they may not have their jobs in a couple years, either because of AI or the other AI known as ‘arrogant immigration.’”

The national-interest argument, though, cuts both ways. At Stanford’s buzzy DEFCON national security conference, one prominent military official spoke of “the relationship between founders, funders, and fighters” as having to be “closer now than it ever has been before.” AI barons could hardly ask for a better invitation to present themselves as indispensable; a president persuaded that national security requires bringing them to heel might just as easily be persuaded that it requires giving them free rein.

Expect this strain of right-wing regulation to gain a louder hearing as the stars align for its move into the mainstream, even if it remains unclear how far Trump might intend to go beyond tougher vibes and support for select bipartisan legislation. Stephen Miller’s chief of staff appointment does little to clarify where the administration is headed. (His wife Katie, an ardent accelerationist, had worked for SpaceX and held shares in the company, requiring him to recuse himself from AI policy. She has since left SpaceX and sold her shares, freeing her husband to shape policy as he takes up his new job.)

The core of Trump’s theory of regulation, though, is well established and unlikely to change. The only “guardrails” AI needs, he wrote on Truth Social in September, are a “STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT.” Nothing in the Douthat interview suggests he’s lost faith in his chosen regulator.

William Liang is a writer living in San Francisco.

articles.title: Crawford: It’s ‘premature’ to place blame on Lutnick for Nvidia chip sales
articles.summary: Rep. Rick Crawford (R-Ark.), chair of the House Intelligence Committee, said Sunday that it is too early to blame Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick for delays in cracking down on companies suspected of illegally funneling Nvidia chips to China after Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent publicly expressed his frustration with the department. “Again, a little premature for…
articles.body:
Rep. Rick Crawford (R-Ark.), chair of the House Intelligence Committee, said Sunday that it is too early to blame Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick for delays in cracking down on companies suspected of illegally funneling Nvidia chips to China after Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent publicly expressed his frustration with the department.

“Again, a little premature for us to be placing blame anywhere, and I think we want to make sure that we have a better understanding of exactly what happened,” Crawford told NewsNation’s “The Hill Sunday.”

Crawford said he and Rep. Jim Himes (Conn.), the top Democrat on the Intelligence Committee, have asked Lutnick to meet with lawmakers on Capitol Hill to explain his department’s actions.

“I do believe he’ll come in and talk to us and give us a little better understanding of what’s taking place,” Crawford said, referring to Lutnick.

His remarks come amid a scandal involving Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who resigned after an alleged affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. Bessent on Friday said he was frustrated with the Commerce Department’s delay in placing export restrictions on Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based company formerly led by Alice Huang, who is suspected by U.S. intelligence of spying for China.

Bessent said the Treasury, State and Defense departments along with the U.S. Trade Representative had all supported placing Megaspeed on a federal export control list for some time, but the Commerce Department had never acted.

“Commerce has the pen, and you will have to ask them about their internal processes,” Bessent told CNBC on Friday. “My deputy has been pushing this for months.”

Asked whether Bessent’s remarks pointed the finger at Lutnick, Crawford on Sunday declined to draw conclusions before hearing directly from the Commerce secretary.

Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Ore.), ranking member of the Senate Finance Committee, and Rep. Richard Neal (Mass.), the top Democrat on the House Ways and Means Committee, separately launched an investigation Thursday into President Trump’s decision to allow Nvidia to sell its powerful H200 chips to China.

The lawmakers demanded that Lutnick preserve records related to the decision, raising concerns about whether political considerations influenced the administration’s export policies.

articles.title: Trump's handpicked party chair faces a rebellion after midterm losses test president's grip on GOP
articles.summary: NEW YORK (AP) — A nascent rebellion is underway against President Donald Trump's handpicked chairman at the Republican National Committee, and it’s already g...
articles.body:
NEW YORK (AP) — A nascent rebellion is underway against President Donald Trump's handpicked chairman at the Republican National Committee, and it's already getting ugly.

Some members are calling for a forensic audit of spending decisions, including hair and makeup services for Trump and other officials, as well as the hiring of the daughter of Trump's former chief of staff. Feuding Republicans are leaking emails and opposition research on rival factions. The White House is threatening to cut off fundraising assistance if the rebels don't fall in line.

The emerging fight, which will shape the 2028 presidential nominating contest, represents a rare challenge to Trump's dominance, even after the party's worst midterm performance in a generation. Despite the broad losses, Republican leaders across Washington have shown little desire to move past Trump and have largely stood behind his most unpopular policies.

But inside the Republican National Committee, an organization of 168 members elected from every state who oversee the party's national political operation, a small and growing collection of concerned Republicans are backing an attempt to depose Joe Gruters. Trump wants to keep him in charge.

The dissidents are rallying behind Kentucky's KC Crosbie, the RNC's second-in-command. She launched her bid just two days after the Nov. 3 election in a letter that drew the fury of both the White House and Gruters' allies.

Crosbie remains a vocal Trump supporter who backs his "Make America Great Again" agenda, but her opponents view her gambit as a direct challenge to the president and his power.

"Our job is to elect Republicans broadly, not to support one man all the time," said RNC member Oscar Brock of Tennessee, who is supporting Crosbie's candidacy. He said that requires a change in leadership because "there's so much frustration that Chairman Gruters didn't pull his weight in this election."

In her letter, Crosbie described the midterms as "a serious setback" and called for the RNC to provide "an honest account" of what went wrong.

The leadership election will be held in January at the RNC's winter meeting in Arizona.

Some would-be Crosbie supporters privately acknowledge they're worried about a backlash from the White House, especially with Stephen Miller taking over as Trump's chief of staff. Others believe in the committee's tradition of having presidents pick their own party chiefs.

Lauren LePage, an RNC member from Maine, praised Gruters' leadership and efforts to help her father, Paul LePage, flip a congressional seat — a rare bright spot for Republicans this cycle.

"From my perspective, as chairman, he did his job," she said, adding that Trump's endorsement is "something that the committee should take very seriously."

The Republicans who have lined up behind Crosbie insist a leadership change is needed to send a clear message that the party will do things differently after losses even in Republican strongholds like Texas , South Carolina and Mississippi .

Patti Lyman, an RNC member from Virginia, said it would be "catastrophic" and "insulting" to the party's base "to keep the same leadership and pretend that we don't need to do anything different, that we don't need new players and a new plan."

Sue Cienki, an RNC committee member from Rhode Island, predicted that Crosbie would have the backing of at least two members from 10 states — a total of 20 — at the committee's January meeting. That's the minimum required for a successful nomination.

Trump and senior White House officials were livid about Crosbie's Nov. 5 letter and the fact that they were given no heads-up. The president soon released a lengthy statement on his Truth Social social media platform hailing Gruters as a "MAGA Warrior" and giving him his "Complete and Total Endorsement."

Trump is expected to play a central role in picking the party's next presidential nominee.

Allies of Gruters say a leadership change now would put the RNC at a severe disadvantage heading into the next presidential cycle because a new team would need time to get up to speed. They say friction between the president and the committee's leadership would curtail their ability to organize and raise money.

They also reject Crosbie's call for a postelection review, which they said would do little more than consume six months rehashing the past and put all their grievances on paper.

Gruters spent much of this week holding private phone conversations with committee members. Those who participated in the calls said Gruters listened to their grievances, but said little about what he would do differently.

The opposition to Gruters has focused on the RNC's spending decisions under him. Republicans had a massive fundraising advantage and still had deep losses.

"There's clearly a groundswell of support for a forensic audit," said Brock, the RNC member from Tennessee.

In a letter to RNC members sent Thursday night and obtained by The Associated Press, Gruters acknowledged concerns about spending and other issues.

Gruters defended a $22,500 expenditure for hospitality space at the Presidents Cup, a golf event, saying the space was offered to major donors and "resulted in $2.5 million in renewed contributions to the RNC."

He also addressed "a brief contract" between the RNC and Caroline Wiles, a longtime Republican consultant, who is the daughter of Susie Wiles, Trump's former chief of staff. Gruters said she was hired by his predecessor at the committee, Michael Whatley.

"While I have no reason to doubt Caroline Wiles's value to the RNC or Chairman Whatley's reasons for bringing her on, this was a brief six-month engagement that ended when I was elected Chairman," he wrote.

Gruters also defended the RNC's decision to pay for "hair and make-up services" for senior White House officials, including Trump, Vice President JD Vance and former press secretary Karoline Leavitt.

"This was a request made of us so that the expense did not fall to taxpayers," Gruters wrote, adding that the beneficiaries "generously gave so much of their limited time and energies to help the RNC this cycle" and "did not ask for much of us in return, so we felt this was a request we could accommodate."

articles.summary: Rep. Greg Stanton (D-Ariz.) on Sunday said the Democratic Party should use the power of the purse to change current U.S. foreign policy regarding Russia. During the Arizona congressman’s appearance on NewsNation’s “The Hill Sunday,” host Chris Stirewalt asked Stanton if it would be a good use of the power of the purse to force…
articles.body:
Rep. Greg Stanton (D-Ariz.) on Sunday said the Democratic Party should use the power of the purse to change current U.S. foreign policy regarding Russia.

During the Arizona congressman’s appearance on NewsNation’s “The Hill Sunday,” host Chris Stirewalt asked Stanton if it would be a good use of the power of the purse to force a government shutdown in order to get President Trump to undo his waiver on Russia sanctions or end the Iran war.

“Well, actually, in a bipartisan way, Congress did pass the Lindsey Graham bill, the bill honoring the deceased senator from South Carolina, Lindsey Graham, to put sanctions on Russia,” Stanton said. “And the president has unilaterally decided not to implement those. But using the power of the purse strings, of course, we’re Congress. We’re an equal branch of government. We are not subservient to Trump.”

In October, Trump issued a controversial executive order that waived energy sanctions against Russia and the top purchasers of Russian energy. Lawmakers had hoped the sanctions legislation would hamper Russian President Vladimir Putin’s ability to fund the war against Ukraine.

“We should use the power of the purse to change American foreign policy. Now that the Democrats are going to be in the majority, you’re going to see American policy more supportive of Ukraine,” Stanton continued.

He alleged that because of the waiver, Trump had “changed sides and was much more supportive of Putin.”

“Too many Republican members of Congress who did support Ukraine stayed silent as he made that change,” the Democratic lawmaker concluded. “Now that we’re in the majority, you’re going to see a significant change in funding priorities from the United States Congress.”

The upcoming budget deadline is Dec. 11, with Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) along with Democratic Sens. Michael Bennet (Colo.), Chris Van Hollen (Md.) and Tammy Duckworth (Ill.) expressing in a joint statement that they will oppose any short-term spending patch that doesn’t include “language that restricts the Trump Administration from using appropriated funds to continue his war against Iran.”

Trump defended his waiver , writing on Truth Social last month that sanctions would have placed Russian hostage negotiations in “ a complete and total halt .” He added the U.S. “was not required to give anything in return” for the release of Stephen Hubbard, a U.S. citizen detained by Russia.

articles.title: Colom urges Democrats to invest more in Mississippi after surprise Senate win
articles.summary: Sen.-elect Scott Colom (D-Miss.) on Sunday called on Democrats to channel more financial and political investment into Mississippi following his surprise Senate win last week. “We didn’t have a bunch of resources. There wasn’t a bunch of campaign money spent to win Mississippi, compared to other states,” Colom said on NBC News’s “Meet the Press.”…
articles.body:
Sen.-elect Scott Colom (D-Miss.) on Sunday called on Democrats to channel more financial and political investment into Mississippi following his surprise Senate win last week.

“We didn’t have a bunch of resources. There wasn’t a bunch of campaign money spent to win Mississippi, compared to other states,” Colom said on NBC News’s “Meet the Press.” “But that meant we did it the Mississippi way, and I’m proud of that. What we need to do now, as a Democratic Party, is understand we can’t continue to allow that lack of investment to occur.”

Colom noted that Democrats “need to put senators like myself in position where we can deliver for the rural South, where we can be leaders in ways that show the voters in rural America that we care about them, the voters in the Deep South that we want them to be successful.”

The Mississippi Democrat joined a roster of incoming Democratic senators-elect who claimed victory in the 2026 midterm elections. The party won Senate seats in Iowa, Kansas, Maine, North Carolina, Ohio, South Carolina and Texas, with Alaska yet to be determined .

He defeated incumbent Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith (R-Miss.) last Wednesday, herself having won the seat in 2020. Hyde-Smith, who was endorsed by President Trump, was favored to win the race.

Colom will be the Magnolia State’s first Black senator since former Sens. Hiram Revels (R-Miss.) and Blanche Kelso Bruce (R-Miss.). Both were elected in the 1870s, in the years before the end of Reconstruction in 1877. But a Democrat has not won the seat since 1982.

“Meet the Press” host Kristen Welker asked Colom where he stands on supporting either Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) or Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.), who is making a bid to be Senate majority leader in the new Congress.

“I’ve got to be honest with you. I don’t know either one of them that well,” he said. “So, I’m going to listen to what other people tell me about them and I’m going to figure out what are the things that people are doing well in leadership, what are the things they’re not doing well, and find out how we can work together to achieve results.”

Democratic strategist Fred Hicks, based in Georgia and Florida, previously told The Hill that the South is “not just winnable; it also completely changes the calculus of the path of victory for the presidency if any Southern states are in play.” He said Democrats should “not cede anything in the South.”

The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC) expanded its battleground with its eyes on Florida, Georgia and Texas this summer. In August, the Democratic National Committee (DNC) launched a Southern States Resource Hub investment, when Chair Ken Martin announced “the puck is heading to the South.”

Along with Colom’s major victory as Mississippi’s first Black senator in more than a century, Georgia and Texas both saw similar historic victories . Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms (D) will be the former’s first Black woman to serve as governor, and Democrat Gina Hinojosa will be the Lone Star State’s first Latina woman chief executive.

articles.body:
President Trump said on Sunday that the Interior Department will appeal a court ruling which barred the Trump administration from closing East Potomac Park this weekend.

“Biden appointed Judge Reyes has delayed, for yet another two weeks, the fix up and reconstruction, by the Department of the Interior, of one of the worst and most dangerous golf courses anywhere in the U.S. ‘Trash Island,’ as it is affectionately known, needs work, and needs it now,” Trump wrote on Truth Social .

“It is in a terrible state of disrepair, as anybody can see by just looking at the pictures that are now circulating all over the Country, and in the Court,” the president continued. “‘INTERIOR’ has the absolute right to do so, and will immediately appeal, on an expedited basis, this highly destructive and political decision of the judge.”

“Time is of the essence, or golf seasons, jobs, prestige, and much money, will be lost,” Trump added.

The decision comes after U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes ruled on Saturday that the park “shall remain open and accessible to the public” except for “routine, temporary closures” that may be needed to address imminent threats to public safety. The Trump administration would still need to give a 24-hour warning to Reyes before working on imminent threats.

Trump took to bashing East Potomac Park in his post, saying it was “mocked all over D.C.(and far beyond!)” and questioned, “why would a judge want to delay taking a terrible and very unsafe golf course…instead of quickly turning it into a great and admired one?”

Reyes’s ruling was a win for critics of the project who noted that the golf course would stretch more than 8,000 yards from the back tees – reducing accessibility for beginner and casual golfers who have long been able to play at East Potomac Park at an affordable price.

The preservationist group and two local golfers who filed the lawsuit also argued that Trump’s renovations were actually a pretext to instead host major professional tournaments at the course.

The judge was not sympathetic to the Justice Department’s (DOJ) argument that renovations were needed for seawall repairs, calling it a “self-inflicted” issue. She pointed out the Trump administration terminated its contract with the nonprofit who maintained the course last year.

“You’re the one who set the house on fire,” she told the DOJ.
