articles.title: FAA ground stop timeline: Weekend chaos grounds planes and postpones games
articles.summary: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said overloaded routers tied to contractor L3Harris maintenance work triggered the longest nationwide FAA ground stop in 25 years.
articles.body: A communications failure brought departures across the country to a halt Friday, stranding travelers, disrupting professional sports teams and sending federal officials scrambling to restore flights and determine what went wrong. The longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years ended after more than four hours, but the fallout stretched through the weekend as airlines worked through cancellations and investigators zeroed in on routers tied to the outage. Here’s a timeline of the shutdown and the federal response. All times are Eastern. 4 CRITICAL TRAVEL ISSUES FOR THOSE DELAYED AND DISRUPTED BY FAA NATIONWIDE GROUND STOP Friday afternoon, Nov. 13: Communications trouble triggers nationwide ground stop Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said officials detected instability in radar data and communications at 3:36 p.m., affecting facilities that guide planes approaching airports and traveling between them. The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) halted departures nationwide at 3:54 p.m. as controllers and pilots followed procedures to bring aircraft already airborne safely to the ground. About 3,500 flights were in the air. FAA SAYS AIR TRAVEL SHOULD BE BACK TO NORMAL SUNDAY AFTER NATIONWIDE GROUND STOP Duffy later emphasized that officials had not lost every radar feed or all telecommunications service. The inconsistent information was enough to trigger the shutdown as a safety precaution. Friday, 4:16 p.m.: Duffy announces investigation into communications problem Duffy said the ground stop was necessary because of "a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers." FAA technicians were investigating, he said. The disruption also prompted a broader federal response as officials examined whether the failure could have involved malicious activity. BUTTIGIEG TAKES SWIPE AT TRUMP ADMINISTRATION AMID FAA FLIGHT CHAOS President Donald Trump brought federal agencies together on a call Friday, including intelligence officials, the FBI and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency. Intelligence partners reported they were not detecting the usual signs of a cyberattack, Duffy said. Steven Cheung, assistant to the president and White House director of communications, later said on X that the White House and administration had acted within minutes of the FAA notice, crediting Trump for the response. UPDATED START TIMES FOR COLLEGE FOOTBALL GAMES AFFECTED BY FAA GROUND STOP, BROKEN DOWN BY CONFERENCE "Minutes after the FAA notice posted, the White House and Administration sprang into action. Because of that speed and effectiveness, the ground stop was lifted after just a few hours," Cheung wrote. "A Herculean effort, only made possible by President Trump's leadership." NFL OFFICIAL DON WILLARD WILL REFEREE TWO GAMES IN ONE DAY AFTER FAA GROUND STOP DISRUPTS TRAVEL, LEAGUE SAYS Friday evening: Officials address security concerns as sports teams are stranded Speaking to reporters outside the White House on Friday, Nov. 13, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was no indication of a nefarious attack and reassured Americans with loved ones traveling. "There’s no reason for the public to be afraid or scared for your loved ones," Mullin said. TENNESSEE VOLUNTEERS OVERCOME SLUGGISH OFFENSE, JET LAG TO TAKE DOWN TEXAS A&M AND KEEP CFP HOPES ALIVE The shutdown also left college football teams scrambling to reach Saturday’s games. Texas had already boarded its plane for Baton Rouge to face LSU when the ground stop prevented departure. Tennessee’s scheduled 4 p.m. flight to College Station was also halted. Teams including Ole Miss, Tennessee and Baylor returned to their athletic facilities as officials weighed alternate travel plans. Some teams sat aboard charter planes for up to two hours. PRIVATE PLANES AND ROADTRIPS: AEW GOES ABOVE AND BEYOND TO GET TO PHOENIX FOR FULL GEAR DESPITE TRAVEL CHAOS The shutdown also disrupted travel for professional sports teams ahead of a busy weekend. The Brooklyn Nets were trying to fly from New Orleans to Memphis when their flight was halted, according to The Associated Press. The Memphis Grizzlies were also in New Orleans for a Friday game against the Pelicans, with plans to depart afterward. The Cleveland Cavaliers and Chicago Bulls also had planned postgame flights. The San Jose Sharks’ flight to Utah for a Saturday game against the Mammoth did not depart before the shutdown, while the Detroit Pistons had reached Miami earlier Friday. Friday, 8:15 p.m.: Ground stop lifted, but recovery starts slowly The FAA lifted the nationwide order at 8:15 p.m., allowing departures to resume. Planes began leaving airports including LaGuardia, Los Angeles International and Reagan National. Some travelers at Reagan National had been waiting since around 3:30 p.m. for flights scheduled to leave around 4 p.m. Duffy warned that reopening the airspace would not immediately get every flight moving. Departures depended on whether airlines had pilots, flight attendants and other crews available. "It’s going to be slow," he said. Late Friday into Saturday: College football games rescheduled Lifting the ground stop did not immediately solve the travel problems for college teams. By 9:12 p.m. Friday, Washington, Texas, Tennessee and Oregon State were heading back to airports, but other programs faced crew availability problems. Utah’s charter crew ran out of available hours, forcing the team to plan a Saturday morning departure for its game at Arizona. The Big 12 moved kickoff to 10:30 p.m. ET Saturday. Just after midnight Saturday, the Ole Miss-Oklahoma game was moved to 1 p.m. ET Sunday after the Rebels were unable to leave Friday evening. Oklahoma athletic director Roger Denny said the school objected to the change but was told it would face a forfeit if it refused to play Sunday. Saturday, Nov. 14: Maintenance work and overloaded routers emerge as focus At a Saturday briefing, Duffy said contractor L3Harris had been replacing aging copper communications lines with fiber-optic connections at a remote FAA location. The copper line was being discontinued, making the replacement necessary, he said. During the work, a router began generating more than 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds, overwhelming other routers and disrupting communications and radar feeds. Investigators were examining whether installation error or faulty equipment caused the failure. "Our contractor didn’t meet the moment or the equipment didn’t meet the moment," Duffy said. Bedford distinguished the routine maintenance from the administration’s broader air traffic control modernization program. Duffy also said officials would reevaluate when such work should be performed. Saturday: Airlines regroup as FAA forecasts Sunday recovery FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said "the worst is behind us," with air travel expected to return to normal by the end of Sunday. The Transportation Department said more than 8,000 flight operations resumed Friday night after the ground stop ended, but passengers continued facing delays and cancellations Saturday. Airlines still needed to reposition aircraft and crews, leaving travelers scrambling to rebook and check whether their flights would operate. Officials urged passengers to check directly with their airlines for current flight information. Sunday, Nov. 15: Router testing continues as Duffy presses for funding Duffy said Sunday morning that air travel would improve throughout the day but probably would not return fully to normal until Monday, updating officials’ earlier prediction of a recovery by Sunday night. Two routers from Texas and Arkansas were undergoing testing as investigators worked to determine the cause. Duffy said work in El Dorado, Arkansas, was followed by problems involving equipment in Amarillo, Texas, where a system had been replaced about three weeks earlier. Engineers were examining the routers at an L3Harris laboratory in Florida. "We think it was the installation or the router that was the bad actor," Duffy said. He said there was no indication of a foreign cyberattack, while leaving open further investigation if new evidence emerged. Duffy also pressed Congress for additional funding. He said the $12.5 billion already allocated covered specific upgrades, including radar, radios and electronic flight strips, but did not fund a replacement telecommunications network. Sunday, 2 p.m.: Travel headaches drag on By 2 p.m. ET Sunday, 5,280 flights had been delayed and 1,709 canceled within, into or out of the U.S., according to FlightAware. Dallas Fort Worth, Atlanta and Chicago O’Hare were among the hardest-hit airports tracked in the update, with hundreds of delays at each. The disruptions continued Sunday afternoon as airlines worked to restore normal schedules. FORMER TOP FAA OFFICIAL WARNS OF 48-HOUR RECOVERY AFTER AGING TECH 'OVERWHELMED' AHEAD OF GROUND STOP Sunday, Nov. 15: United CEO calls for action United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby praised the FAA’s decision to halt flights and thanked employees and customers for their patience during the disruption. He also called for better technology and full staffing to help prevent future outages. Kirby said he had spoken directly with Duffy, Bedford and aviation leaders from both parties in Congress about the impact on United’s passengers and employees. "This moment must be a call to action," Kirby said in a statement shared with Fox News Digital. "It is critical for safety, our passengers, and our economy that we fix our nation’s Air Traffic Control system now." Kirby said lawmakers from both parties were committed to modernizing the system while holding the FAA accountable. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Fox News' Grady Trimble, Anders Hagstrom, Stephen Sorace, Trey Wallace, and The Associated Press contributed to this report.

articles.title: Texas prosecutor accuses Warren of targeting Trump associates with investigations
articles.summary: A federal prosecutor in Texas warned Sen. Aaron Reitz (R), the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of Texas, accused Warren of preparing to…
articles.body:
A federal prosecutor in Texas warned Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) on Sunday of potential legal consequences over her plans to investigate President Trump and his allies, demanding that she preserve documents related to her upcoming congressional oversight efforts.

Aaron Reitz (R), the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of Texas, accused Warren of preparing to target those associated with Trump when she takes over as chair of the Senate Banking Committee next year.

In a letter to Warren posted on the social platform X , Reitz described the senator as being “on the warpath to wield her committee gavel like a tomahawk, seeking the scalps of those who associate ‘too closely’ with President Trump.”

Reiz’s letter and accompanying social media post references Trump’s multiple attacks against Warren over her past claims of Native American heritage.

“Congressional investigations can’t be used to punish Americans for exercising their 1A rights,” he wrote in a post on X accompanying the letter. “My first arrow shot.”

The letter referenced Warren’s Nov. 8 appearance on CBS News’s “Face the Nation,” nearly one week after the midterm elections, where Warren said Democrats would pursue investigations after reclaiming control of Congress in the midterm elections.

“If you’ve been making your profits by cheating American families and scamming your investors, you better get ready for some investigations, serious ones,” Warren told host Margaret Brennan.

Reitz, a former chief of staff to Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas), argued that those remarks sent a “strong smoke signal” that Warren intended to target private individuals close to Trump.

“You are obligated to preserve all potentially relevant evidence related to your efforts to suppress associational activities related to President Trump and the Trump Administration,” he wrote, adding failure to do so may result in legal consequences.

Reitz gave Warren, who has not been accused of a crime, until Nov. 23 to confirm that she received the letter and preserved the requested records. He issued similar warnings last week to Sens. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) and Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.).

The White House also backed Reitz’s latest warning Sunday, accusing Democrats of preparing to pursue politically motivated investigations.

“Democrats like Elizabeth Warren are looking to weaponize their positions against people who are simply close to President Trump or work with him,” White House communications director Steven Cheung wrote on X . “This is nothing more than an extension of their political witch-hunt that has gone on for far too long.”

articles.body:
Rep.-elect Dan Koh (D-Mass.) on Sunday blamed President Trump for blocking more than $1 trillion in Biden-era funding for infrastructure and funds toward the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), referring to Friday’s rare nationwide ground stop for all U.S. flights.

Koh joined the panel on MS NOW’s “The Weekend” as part of a discussion on Trump’s claim on Truth Social Sunday morning that the Biden administration made “an old and broken system” at the FAA “worse than when they began,” and called for Congress “to give the money, FAST!”

“Well, first of all, it’s kind of revisionist history,” Koh replied to co-host Eugene Daniels. “I mean, you might as well start blaming Ronald Reagan for the FAA strike in ’80s as part of this too. I mean, look, it’s absurd.”

“President Biden had historic funding, not only to the FAA, but over a trillion dollars worth of infrastructure money, a lot of it that Donald Trump has reversed on the grounds of it being too woke,” Koh continued.

The Massachusetts Democrat said that in his talks with mayors and city council members expecting to see this funding enter the communities and upgrade aspects like transportation, “they don’t even know if they’re going to get any more because the administration has not even gotten back to them on the status.”

He agreed that he would “absolutely” approve for more FAA funding “if it helps.”

“But I don’t see this as a president who’s actually genuine in his intentions, and certainly doesn’t have a track record of doing something,” Koh added.

Trump on Sunday called on Congress to provide the “desperately needed money for Air Traffic Control, we can get it built quickly and efficiently,” he wrote on Truth Social, adding that it “will be the BEST SYSTEM anywhere in the World.”

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) on Friday afternoon issued a ground stop. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy asked for $50 billion , noting Trump’s prior request for $30 billion.

Biden signed a $1.2 trillion bipartisan infrastructure bill in November 2021 that allocated $25 billion in funding toward the FAA to improve its airports and traffic control towers, among other updates.

It also contained $550 billion in new federal spending invested over five years, with funds intended for improving roads and bridges, as well as expanding broadband access.

Trump signed an executive order days after returning to the White House pausing the disbursement of funds appropriated through the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law. The order was unclear to lawmakers, as the pause only applied to funds “supporting programs, projects or activities that may be implicated by the policy established,” according to one part of the order.

What was unclear is whether it included money committed by the federal government that hasn’t officially been released. Sen. John Hoeven (R-N.D.) told The Hill at the time that it was Republicans trying “to claw back funds there.”
